Business.title: EU to impose cap on Chinese hybrid EV imports next month
Business.text:
The EU will next month impose its threatened caps on the number of Chinese hybrid cars that can be imported into the bloc, the European Commission has announced.

The quotas will also apply to hybrids from Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the UK, but the principal purpose is to limit imports from China after an agreement with Beijing in October that has led to a rise in exports to the bloc.

The quota, under World Trade Organization rules, is temporary and will apply for 200 days from 1 December during an investigation into imports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid vehicles. The EU is attempting to cut its huge trade deficit with China.

“In view of the sensitivity of the hybrids sector, its strategic importance to the union economy in terms of innovation, electrification and employment, and the existence of sufficient evidence showing that imports of hybrids threaten to cause serious injury to the union industry,” the official journal said on Tuesday.

It will limit tariff-free imports of Chinese vehicles to 350,000 in the first year or about 191,000 over 200 days.

First-year quotas would be set at 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK, which last year exported 166,000 hybrids to the EU.

The quota amounts to about half of the number of Chinese hybrids expected to be imported to the EU in the next 12 months.

Figures in the journal showed that imports of Chinese EVs rocketed from 21,000 units in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024 when tariffs were imposed.

After the tariffs were imposed, imports of EVs began to “flatten out”, with a “clear shift” from EVs to hybrids from China, it said.

Worldwide exports of hybrids from China rocketed from 191,000 vehicles in 2023 to 1.124m in 2025, the EU said.

To head off “the likelihood of substantially increased imports into the union”, the EU now is imposing a quota.

The volume limits are “safeguard” measures that have to apply to all big exporters of ‌hybrid cars to the EU. Other countries to which the import caps apply are South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Serbia and the US, but they are most restrictive for China.

According to industry reports, non-EU countries including the UK have questioned the allocations.

At a WTO goods council meeting last week, South Korea questioned whether the investigation was fair and transparent. Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Turkey stressed transparency and due process.

China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by the consensus the two sides had reached, and that it reserved all rights to firmly safeguard the legitimate interests of Chinese industries.

The European Commission said imports from China came not just at the expense of EU production, but were also eating into the market shares of other exporters such as Japan and South Korea.

Business.title: Wild stock market swings: will I lose money, and is there anything I can do?
Business.text:
Will I lose money?

Lots of people own shares that are falling in value, either through their pension or other type of investment account. Many of the shares that are experiencing the biggest falls are companies that have dominated indices and, as a result, the passive funds that track them.

Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, says two of the most popular passive investments among investors are global equity funds and funds tracking the S&P 500 US stock market index. “Both have exposure to the giants of tech in a large way,” he says. And, as a result, both have fallen in recent days.

Coatsworth says that, while 15 years ago US shares represented half of the MSCI World index – a benchmark for the global stock market – it is now 73%. Tech is the dominant sector and officially represents 30% of the index. However, Google’s parent Alphabet and Facebook’s owner Meta are classed as communication services stocks – adding them bumps up tech to about 35% of the index.

Investors who think they have diversified by being in a global fund may be having a nasty surprise.

The investment platform interactive investor (ii) reports on the top holdings of its customers every quarter. Its most recent report shows global tracker funds are well-represented in their portfolios, as is Scottish Mortgage – an actively managed investment trust that holds shares in SpaceX, Nvidia and Anthropic, among others.

However, an important thing to remember about falling share prices is that you do not lose money until you sell. Only at that point do you crystallise your loss.

And you may not even have losses on paper, depending on when you invested. In recent years stock markets have been climbing. The FTSE 100 is still higher than it was last year. Scottish Mortgage has been falling since mid-October, but its shares are still well up on this time last year.

How do I diversify to avoid further tech downturns?

Coatsworth says there are a few paths to consider.

“One way to dial down tech exposure is to switch into a global equity fund that excludes the US,” he says. “For example, iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.”

Tech stocks outside the US account for 10.9% of the portfolio, but the main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners. “That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat,” he says. However, if those stocks recover, you will be missing out on any potential gains.

He says a possible “middle ground” is the Invesco MSCI World Equal Weight ETF. At the end of September, the US represented 40.6% of the investment – less than with a traditional global equity fund. “The investor still has their toe in the pond for US tech exposure, but they wouldn’t be up to their neck in the water,” he says.

Business.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
Business.text:
Invoking Greek mythology, the US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, by which the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders were either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Business.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
Business.text:
Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide, although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals.

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. They immediately spun this to the media, suggesting that all software, everywhere, is extraordinarily vulnerable to AI-driven hacking – and offering their tools to banks and spying agencies.

Some have argued that this hype is not entirely justified, suggesting that many vulnerabilities these models discover are not particularly useful to hackers. But the threat of AI-driven hacking has changed the game.

One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer, a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip.

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items, as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

More troubling hacks, and more conspiracy theories, are probably on the horizon. The senior cybersecurity professional said heightened public awareness of cyber disruption had led to hypersensitivity about any incident.

“It’s like the tide has gone out on cybersecurity in terms of public perception, and there’s the same amount of wrecks out there as there have been for years. Any time you change a complex system, stuff happens.”

However, the professional is concerned that AI, with its capacity to identify flaws, help plan attacks and execute them, will be harnessed by “already very competent” adversaries. Referring to the general state of IT security around the world, the source added: “Thank goodness we haven’t had an AI-sourced vulnerability that is easy to exploit. Because that would be carnage.”

For many, though, recent events have been bad enough.

When Josephine’s* prescription request for lithium for her bipolar disorder was lost “in the ether” during the global Microsoft outage, she admits she was “freaking out”.

“My medication is life-changing and keeps me stable,” said the 26-year-old, a student living in the east of England. After an agonising wait, she was finally able to collect her prescription, but the experience has left her deeply troubled.

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

* Name has been changed

Additional reporting by Jane Clinton

Sports.title: World Cup and Clarkson partnership drove profit surge, says Marston's
Sports.text:
Pub company Marston's has said an "excellent World Cup" helped drive stronger trading as annual profits rose by nearly a fifth, despite reporting a dip in sales.

The Wolverhampton-based firm, which operates more than 1,300 pubs across the UK, reported underlying pre-tax profits of £85.4m for the year to 26 September, up 18.4% from a year earlier.

The company said trading was improved by new-look pubs, strong trade during this summer's football World Cup, and a partnership with Jeremy Clarkson's Hawkstone drinks brand.

"For the third year running, profit is significantly up, cash flow is strong and margins have improved," said chief executive Justin Platt.

The pub chain also said bookings for Christmas events were 9% ahead of the same point last year.

Marston's has invested heavily in refurbishing pubs into new formats, including its sports-focused "Grandstand" venues.

It plans at least 100 more conversions in the new financial year, in a bid to accelerate sales growth further.

One of the busiest locals during the World Cup was The New Spires in Coventry, which reopened in March following a £400,000 makeover.

Marston's also pointed to events and promotions, including darts champion Luke Humphries' darts nights and the partnership with Clarkson.

"Guest satisfaction levels have improved again, thanks to the amazing work of our pub teams, whose passion and commitment keep our pubs at the heart of every local community they serve," added Platt.

"Our new pub formats are performing especially well and are now a proven growth engine for the business, giving us real confidence to accelerate our investment plans in 2027."

Sports.title: Leny Yoro red card: Mauricio Pochettino leads Manchester United fury at VAR ruling
Sports.text:
Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has questioned the competence of video assistant referee officials after defender Leny Yoro had his red card overturned by the Football Association.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United's 4-0 defeat at Liverpool on Sunday after bringing down Aleksander Isak just outside the United penalty area.

United sources say they have conclusive proof it was impossible for Isak to reach the ball after he took a heavy touch, that it would have run on to goalkeeper Senne Lammens and Yoro should not have been punished for denying a goalscoring opportunity.

Pochettino said he had some sympathy with referee Sam Barrott but he is livid at how the situation played out.

"I am very disappointed," the Argentine said. "This type of thing can never happen.

"We can accept the referee can make a mistake. But if we have VAR, what were they doing? What were they doing? Are we going to repeat the game? Are we going to have the possibility to play 11 by 11? No.

"We have an unbelievable car, but we need to be at the level to drive [it]. We accept that the technology is there but what are they doing?"

United are furious at both the nature of the audio of the incident, and referees' chief Howard Webb defending referee Barrott's decision and the VAR John Brooks' reinforcing it on the Mic'd Up programme, which was shown on Sky Sports.

They intend to take the matter up with both the Premier League and ProRef.

It is the second time this season United been on the wrong end of a major VAR error.

Webb apologised to United after Erling Haaland's winner in the Manchester derby at Old Trafford on 13 September was allowed to stand even though a clearly offside Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play.

There has been no apology from Webb on this occasion.

Instead, he has doubled down on the call, saying: "I think, by and large, most people would see that as a correct decision, with Isak moving quickly on towards that ball."

United sources claim this interpretation is wrong.

The club are unhappy at the speed the on-field decision was confirmed. It is thought United used data around Isak's top speed and his chances of reaching the ball in their defence of Yoro to the FA. They claim this could have been done "within minutes" of the incident occurring.

This is not the only bone of contention at Old Trafford around the incident.

Pochettino also pointed out Liverpool forward Bradley Barcola was too close to the United wall from the resulting free-kick and Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal should have been disallowed.

"No-one talked about [the fact] that the goal wasn't legal," said Pochettino. "Barcola was touching our wall. It must be disallowed.

"We need to defend my players and my club, and that is to denounce it and to say, the decision wasn't good. And now, the three points, where are the three points?"

Sports.title: Afcon 2025 final verdict: Senegal reinstated as winners by Cas
Sports.text:
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.

With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.

Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.

That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.

Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.

In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.

A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."

The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".

"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.

"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."

Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".

Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".

The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.

A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.

First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.

The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.

Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.

Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.

Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

They eventually returned, but over 15 minutes had elapsed since the award of the penalty by the time Real Madrid's Diaz failed to convert, with his Panenka-style attempt easily saved by goalkeeper Edouard Mendy.

Meanwhile, there was unrest inside the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium as a small contingent of Senegal supporters clashed with security staff.

The game went into extra time, with midfielder Gueye scoring the goal which settled the contest in Senegal's favour.

Off the pitch, another match involving disciplinary boards and lawyers would soon begin.

Senegal celebrated their second continental title but the FRMF quickly lodged an appeal with Caf, arguing their opponents had breached Article 82 of Afcon regulations, which covers withdrawals.

It states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".

A disciplinary board from the continental game's governing body rejected the FRMF's appeal days after the final as it sanctioned and fined those found guilty of unsporting conduct during the match.

Yet in March, almost two months on from the final, a Caf appeals board ruled that Senegal had forfeited the match and awarded Morocco a 3-0 victory.

The FSF described the ruling as "unfair, unprecedented and unacceptable" and swiftly lodged its case with Cas.

The director general of the Switzerland-based court said arbitration proceedings would be conducted "as swiftly as possible", but it was over five months until all parties descended on Lausanne for a one-day hearing.

The Cas panel was led by Frenchman Gerald Simon, founder of the Sports Law Laboratory at the University of Burgundy and a Cas member for 23 years.

Both the FRMF and FSF were able to nominate an arbitrator to exercise an independent judicial function once their appointment was confirmed.

The FRMF nominated Italian international law professor Luigi Fumagalli, while the FSF nominated Hamburg-based attorney and professor of ​law at the University of Zurich Ulrich Haas. Those two men completed the Cas panel.

Over six weeks on from that hearing - and 10 months since the Afcon 2025 final - Senegal have been proclaimed champions once again.

But the debate and damage done to the reputation of African football is likely to linger for some time yet.

Despite Cas being the highest authority in sport, and its decision coming 10 months on from the final, there could yet be a further twist.

The FRMF raised a grievance with the process before the panel's judgement was announced on Tuesday.

It alleged that German attorney Haas, the arbitrator on the panel nominated by the Senegalese, held a telephone call with FSF president Abdoulaye Fall on Sunday.

Fall "categorically" denies that any such phone call ever took place.

The FRMF says that any unauthorised communication between a member of the panel and one of the interested parties would constitute a serious breach of Cas regulations.

It has demanded that "appropriate legal consequences be applied to actions that compromise the integrity and credibility of the arbitration process".

The Moroccans could appeal against the ruling by taking the case to the Swiss Federal Tribunal, and the country's highest court could set Cas' judgement aside.

The case would then likely be heard again at Cas, with a different panel in place.

A precedent would be the case of Chinese swimmer Sun Yang, who had an appeal against the decision by Cas to impose an eight-year doping ban upheld by the Swiss Federal Tribunal.

A new panel heard his case at Cas, and his ban was reduced to four years and three months.

Sports.title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi: 15-year-old smashes the record for the fastest List A double century
Sports.text:
India's 15-year-old batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hit the most sixes ever recorded in a senior men's innings in blazing 204 from 53 balls for India A against the United Arab Emirates.

While almost halving the record for the fastest double-century in List A cricket, Sooryavanshi hit 28 sixes and seven fours in the Asia Cup Rising Stars competition - easily breaking Chad Bowes' previous record of 103 balls from 2024.

The teenage opener also broke the record for the fastest century and 150, the latter of which he already held, before being caught at long-off with his side five runs from victory.

India A ultimately passed their target of 250, played against a UAE side that featured a number of internationals but was not their current first-choice side, in 14.2 overs in Doha.

Sooryavanshi now holds the following records in List A cricket, the categorisation given to senior one-day matches:

Fastest fifty: 11 balls v Sri Lanka A, 21 June (previously Kaushalya Weeraratne, 12 balls, 1 November 2005)

Fastest hundred: 28 balls, today (previously Jake Fraser-McGurk, 29 balls, 8 October 2023)

Fastest 150: 40 balls, today (previously himself, 59 balls, 24 December 2025)

Fastest 200: 52 balls, today (previously Chad Bowes, 103 balls, 22 October 2024)

The previous record for the most sixes in senior matches was 26, struck by Tanmay Agarwal in an innings of 366 for Hyderabad against Arunachal Pradesh in India's first-class Ranji Trophy competition in January 2024.

The record in List A cricket was 23 sixes, struck by D'Arcy Short for Queensland in his 257 against Tasmania on 28 September 2018.

Sooryavanshi also holds the records of being the youngest century-maker in both List A and T20 cricket and the youngest captain in T20s.

"The first thing that's required in this format is being fearless, he's got plenty of that," former India batter Deep Dasgupta told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Technically he's quite unique. There is a tendency of being over-coached in this generation, there's so many coaches and when you start playing franchise cricket.

"The best part is he has been fast-tracked so he hasn't had a lot of coaches, he's kind of untouched. What you see of him is predominantly what his natural game is.

"That bat swing, the hand speed, which is very, very natural and one of the quickest you'll come across. Technically he's very gifted, he's very special and he's definitely the real deal."

Sooryavanshi has rapidly become a sensation in T20 cricket since making his debut in the Indian Premier League in 2025 at the age of 14.

He has hit two hundreds and six fifties in his first two seasons in the competition and has earned 10 caps for India in the shortest format since making his debut against England in July.

The left-hander, who was batting in only his 16th List A innings in Doha and made his second century in the format, is yet to play for India in 50-over cricket.

He put on partnerships of 68 with opening partner Abhishek Sharma, who scored 12, 40 with Prabhsimran Singh, who added just three, and 137 with Rinku Singh, who scored an unbeaten 27.

The India A side, which featured a number of internationals, restricted the UAE to 249-8 in 50 overs, external after their opposition had chosen to bat and swiftly reached 254-3 to win by seven wickets and guarantee their place in the semi-finals.

The Rising Stars competition features A sides from India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Afghanistan alongside squads from the UAE, Nepal and Hong Kong.

India A, who now top Group B, beat Nepal and lost to Pakistan A in their previous two matches in the competition, with Sooryavanshi making scores of 26 and 11.

Pakistan A will retake the top spot if they beat Nepal on Tuesday, with semi-finals on Thursday and Friday to follow before Sunday's final.

Sports.title: Jannik Sinner: World number two has 'minor' surgery on knee after lengthy injury absence
Sports.text:
World number two Jannik Sinner says he has had "minor surgery" on his knee, just seven weeks before January's Australian Open begins.

The five-time Grand Slam champion has not played competitively since winning Wimbledon on 12 July.

In a post on Instagram, Sinner said he had undergone surgery to "improve the condition of my iliotibial band" - a thick band of tissue that runs along the outside of the knee.

"Over the past few months, together with my team we've tried everything to treat my injury without surgery," the 25-year-old wrote.

"After some very encouraging progress early on, my knee unfortunately didn't respond as we'd all hoped.

"I really miss being on court and will now begin my recovery process together with my team."

Earlier in November, Sinner said his goal was to go to Australia and potentially "play a few tournaments" before the first Grand Slam of the year begins on 17 January.

However, the Italian has also stressed the need to think of his long-term career in protecting his body.

The Instagram post is the first time Sinner has specified what the knee issue is.

In a video posted on his Youtube channel in October, Sinner said he had also lost "a lot of weight" after having his tonsils removed.

He also described having "days where I felt nothing and could play without any problems, and then days where I couldn't move at all".

He suffered a nasty fall in the first match of his Wimbledon title defence and also had blood seeping through his shoes because of a problematic toenail.

Alexander Zverev has become world number one in Sinner's absence, while rival Carlos Alcaraz swept four titles after returning from his injury lay-off in September.

Sinner was the dominant player for the first half of the season, winning 44 and losing just three of his singles matches.

He won five Masters 1000 titles in a row between March and May, becoming the youngest man to complete the 'career Golden Masters', and reclaimed the world's top ranking from Alcaraz along the way.

However, he suffered a shock second-round exit at the French Open, with Zverev ultimately stepping up to win his first Grand Slam title.

Sinner bounced back on the grass courts, demolishing Novak Djokovic in the semi-finals before coming back from a set down against Zverev in the Wimbledon showpiece.

He ended his season in early October, meaning he was unable to defend the points he claimed with title triumphs in China, Vienna, Paris and the ATP Finals at the end of 2025.

Zverev went on to win the US Open and secure the year-end number one ranking.

Having met in three of the four Grand Slam finals last year, Sinner and Alcaraz played each other only once in 2026.

Sinner won their final at the Monte Carlo Masters shortly before Alcaraz spent four months out with a wrist injury.

Alcaraz's victory at the season-ending ATP Finals means he is only 350 ranking points behind Sinner - although the Spaniard will be defending 2,000 of those at the Australian Open.

"It's a shame we don't have Jannik," Alcaraz told SuperTennis TV, external after winning the ATP Finals on Sunday.

"We really miss him. I have not seen him for many months right now since I got injured in April.

"I can't wait to see him fit, healthy. I am pretty sure that he is going to come back even better and stronger."

Alcaraz will be the defending champion in Melbourne, having beaten Djokovic to complete a historic career Grand Slam in January.

Sports.title: Louis Rees-Zammit: Wales wing hitting new levels as 2.0 version
Sports.text:
Australia wing Harry Potter had Louis Rees-Zammit exactly where he wanted him.

As Wales attacked in Cardiff on Saturday, Potter showed Rees-Zammit the outside – a four-metre channel between him and the touchline.

The touchline is a defender's best friend. An extra defender. The edge of the cliff. It would take something extraordinary to beat Potter without running out of ground.

A shake of the hips and a change of direction later, Potter was diving like a cricketer in the outfield, grasping at thin air. Rees-Zammit was on his way to setting up a wonderful try for Blair Murray.

Rees-Zammit has been turning heads for years. On the pitch with his pace, off it with his pristine teeth and pop star looks.

But it wasn't raw speed that had left Potter on the turf.

This was Rees-Zammit 2.0 - more than just speed.

Alex Cuthbert knows a thing or two about running. A former national-level 400m runner and British and Irish Lions wing, he spent much of his rugby career working on his technique.

What fascinates him about Rees-Zammit now is not his speed but how he generates it.

"His leg drive and strength from his knee to his hip has got so much stronger," said Cuthbert, who scored 17 tries in 57 Tests for Wales.

The difference is most apparent not over 100 metres but over four or five, changing direction and accelerating before a defender can adjust his feet.

"If you do that shimmy and you stand any sort of player up, you can't recover. Literally can't recover," Cuthbert said.

Cuthbert attributes much of that development to Rees-Zammit's 18 months in American football with the Kansas City Chiefs and Jacksonville Jaguars.

"I thought last season he was a little bit heavy. He looked like a running back last year, whereas this year he is more of a wide receiver," Cuthbert said.

A running back, says Cuthbert, powers through traffic, a wide receiver thrives in open space. He now sees elements of both in Rees-Zammit.

Rees-Zammit's coach at Bristol Bears, Pat Lam, estimates he returned from America eight or nine kilograms heavier.

"What was very clear was his pace was still there, if not quicker, but he was a bigger man and he needed to adjust," said Lam.

Lam is arguably one of rugby's most system-driven coaches. Understanding your role is fundamental at Bristol, where only a select few are afforded the freedom to deviate from the script.

Having established himself as a wing before his American adventure, Rees-Zammit was keen to experiment on his return to rugby.

"He spoke to me about a desire to play full-back and give full-back a go," said Lam.

Lam sees the modern full-back as an auxiliary centre in attack, responsible for creating opportunities for others.

Rees-Zammit's greatest gift is exploiting them.

"But we had to go through that process for him to actually say to me, 'Pat, I'm a world-class winger and I'm a world-class finisher'. And I said, 'I agree'," Lam said.

According to Lam, Rees-Zammit now considers himself a wing who can cover full-back, rather than a full-back who can play on the wing.

Another moment from Saturday offered a reminder of Rees-Zammit's extraordinary pace when Joseph-Aukuso Sua'ali'i intercepted a Welsh pass and set off downfield.

The Australian, a formidable athlete in his own right, had a head start of at least five metres.

One commentator confidently declared he would not be caught.

Rees-Zammit caught him.

The speed has always been there. The numbers reveal how much more there is to his game now.

Rees-Zammit scored five tries in 10 Premiership appearances for Bristol last season. This season he has matched that tally in five games, beating 28 defenders and making 12 clean breaks.

Against Japan earlier in November, he beat 13 defenders and made more line breaks in 80 minutes than in the entire Six Nations, when he started all five games at full-back.

But Rees-Zammit is not the only thing that has changed since March, Wales have changed too

Even the quickest wing in the world is of limited use if he receives the ball standing still with two defenders in front of him.

"But as a winger, you do rely on your boys inside you," said Cuthbert.

With Wales generating more momentum up front, Cuthbert highlights Blair Murray's ability to engage defenders before releasing Rees-Zammit.

Wales are also deploying both wings on the same side of the field. Rees-Zammit and Josh Adams combining for full-back Murray's try was a fine example.

Scrum-half Tomos Williams has perfected the art of the sharp, accurate pass that bypasses players and gets the ball into the wider channels early.

It helped create Rees-Zammit's try against New Zealand and, eight minutes into Saturday's game against the Wallabies, looked to have created another.

Having dived for the corner, Rees-Zammit's first instinct on getting to his feet was not to celebrate or appeal to the referee, but to fix his hair.

The try would not survive the television replays. The hair had survived the tackle.

Image matters to Rees-Zammit. He is Welsh rugby's most marketable player, its biggest draw. He puts bums on seats and gets people out of them.

There is a lovely soundtrack to Rees-Zammit receiving the ball in space at the Principality Stadium. A low hum of excitement followed by the rattle of thousands of seats folding up almost simultaneously.

The thrill is in the anticipation, and these days there is rather more to anticipate.

Sports.title: Jamal Musiala: Bayern Munich hold talks over midfielder's health
Sports.text:
Bayern Munich are only focused on getting Jamal Musiala back from injury and are not interested in the comments made regarding his contract, the club's sporting director Max Eberl insisted.

The 23-year-old collapsed twice in four days during pre-season and said he had been diagnosed with "easily treatable absence seizures, which are due to a neurological dysfunction".

Last week, players' union Fifpro said Bayern Munich's hierarchy "should know better" after the club's honorary president Uli Hoeness said the midfielder may never "regain the performance level he once had".

Describing the talks on Tuesday as "very, very constructive", Eberl said the focus was on Musiala's recovery from a recent injury.

"Today it was about just how we want to get Jamal back on the field, just like before his muscle injury in the international break," Eberl said.

"That's the only task FC Bayern has currently, to give Jamal this trust and not some topics about money or something."

The Bundesliga club's chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen questioned the lucrative contract extension the Germany international signed in 2025, running until 2030, if Musiala fails to get back to his best form, while his predecessor Karl-Heinz Rummenigge suggested the deal, external may need to be renegotiated.

Bayern manager Vincent Kompany said in September it wouldn't be "a big deal" if the seizures return.

Musiala, previously a regular starter and one of the best young talents in Europe, has played five times this season, scoring twice.

"Contracts are there to be respected," Fifpro said on Saturday. "An injury or a dip in form gives a club no grounds to reopen terms it agreed to, just as a run of outstanding performances gives a player no automatic right to a pay rise."

Sports.title: Australia vs England: Aneurin Donald and Phil Salt star as visitors level T20 series
Sports.text:
Second T20, Carrara

Australia 184-8 (20 overs): Chaudhary 45 (35); Curran 2-29

England 188-2 (13.1 overs): Donald 85 (32); Meredith 1-18

England won by eight wickets; series level 1-1

From Gorseinon to the Gold Coast to global recognition.

Welshman Aneurin Donald's demolition of Australia in the second T20 will make the rest of the world notice his talents and pave the way for numerous franchise deals, according to former England captain Michael Vaughan.

Donald's astonishing opening partnership of 151 in 10 overs with Phil Salt helped England hammer Australia and levelled the T20 series on the Gold Coast, as they chased 184 in just 13.1 overs.

Donald blitzed 85 from 32 balls, including nine sixes, while his compatriot Salt made 58 off 30 as the pair from small Welsh villages in Swansea and Denbighshire took the Australians apart.

Donald's 18-ball fifty was the joint third-fastest for England in the format as the pair raced to 79-0 in the powerplay, flogging Australia's second-string bowling attack to all corners of the ground in a remarkable display of power hitting.

"It was a night where we saw a player really step up to the big stage," Vaughan told BBC Sport.

"I'm sure we're going to see much more over the next few years from Donald, but I think tonight the rest of the world noticed and said 'oh, there's a player there'.

"He's got a few franchise gigs at the moment but to do it on the biggest stage against Australia, with the world watching, he's going to be talked about."

His opening partner Salt, who was dropped by Joel Davies on 10, was mostly able to watch from the non-striker's end before accelerating to a 24-ball half-century of his own, which came during a brutal over from spinner Davies that went for 31.

Donald looked gutted to miss out on a century after he holed out to long-on off Riley Meredith's bowling, before Salt was brilliantly caught and bowled by Ben Dwarshuis an over later.

However, England's phenomenal top order - which still awaits the return of Jos Buttler from injury - finished the job with ease as Tom Banton walked off unbeaten on 26 off eight balls, including a monstrous six for the winning runs.

Australia's 184-8 looked competitive on a surface that had assisted England's spinners and Sam Curran's slower balls - the hosts recovering from a stodgy middle over period after falling to 58-4 in the powerplay.

Davies added a handy cameo of 38 before Dwarshuis whacked Curran's last three balls for six to finish strongly but within just a few overs of the chase, Donald and Salt had silenced a lively Australian crowd in style.

The five-match series continues at the Gabba, Brisbane, on Friday.

Donald made his T20 international debut as a 29-year-old earlier this summer on the back of consistent county and Hundred performances, but struggled to really cement his place with 56 runs in four innings.

Still, a player known for an incredible strike-rate in particular, he was backed by Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum to play freely and showcased that strength against an Australia attack that had no answers.

"He's the perfect T20 striker," Vaughan added.

"He has got a great base and a good eye and he doesn't over-complicate it. His mindset is to just try and hit everything for six, very much the modern T20 player.

"The game is moving forward and you need players like Donald who can hit the ball like that."

Brook himself said he was "speechless" at the end of the game, high praise from one of the world's best, as Donald and Salt made what could have been a tricky chase look like a stroll in the park.

Only three international T20s had been held at the Gold Coast's Carrara Oval previously so England were in relatively unknown territory.

Not that it mattered to Donald, who swatted Davies for four from his first ball to start the demolition.

His first couple of sixes off Jack Edwards sailed into the crowd despite looking like he had not timed them perfectly, giving Australia captain Mitch Marsh an insight into his new Perth Scorchers team-mate when the Big Bash League starts in December.

Though the pitch had looked difficult to face spin in Australia's innings, Donald and Salt both tucked into it with aplomb - before Salt's takedown of Davies, Donald clubbed Nikhil Chaudhary for 26 to bring up his fifty by the end of the fifth over.

Donald's showcase gives England a nice headache at the top of the order, with Buttler and Jacob Bethell still to come back into the fold - a frightening prospect for opposition bowlers.

Sports.title: Football gossip: Collins, Tanaka, Calvert-Lewin, Kroupi, Ngumoha, Hudson-Odoi, Hall, Albert
Sports.text:
Manchester United target Brentford defender Nathan Collins, Bournemouth price forward Eli Junior Kroupi at £100m and Liverpool close in on new Rio Ngumoha contract.

Manchester United have Brentford and Republic of Ireland centre-back Nathan Collins, 25, high on their list of January targets (TalkSport), external

Sports.title: Debbie Hewitt signs NDA after viewing documents on failed Fifa sell-off plot
Sports.text:
Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt has signed a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) as a condition of viewing documents related to Fifa president Gianni Infantino's failed World Cup sell-off plot.

Hewitt was granted access to the information at the world governing body's headquarters in Zurich.

Earlier this month, Fifa said "key documents" on the abandoned plan to sell stakes in its tournaments to private investors would be made available to members of its council, but only in person and under "strict review protocols to preserve confidentiality".

Uefa had demanded Fifa release details about the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and answer questions relating to its decision-making.

Hewitt was among a group of council members who wrote to Fifa to say they were "concerned that any review would seemingly be limited to certain 'key documents'… which in turn would only be available for review under unknown 'strict review protocols'".

They also asked for clarity on what the protocols were, and "an explanation as to why Fifa considers such restrictions necessary since it is not clear why our rights are being limited in such a way".

The NDA means Hewitt cannot reveal what she has read, or comment about it publicly.

Fair Square, which campaigns for greater accountability in sport, told BBC Sport: "Debbie Hewitt and the FA didn't need to see the details of FFE to know that it was a gross abuse of presidential power.

"As a member association, the FA is entitled to hold the Fifa president accountable for his actions, and as a Fifa Council vice-president, Hewitt should have seen these plans as soon as they were hatched.

"They had the right to demand to see these documents, and should have exercised that right forcefully and publicly, rather than signing a gagging clause that puts Fifa and Infantino back in control."

Sports.title: Liverpool news: Jurgen Klopp advice and Andoni Iraola confidence helps turn Florian Wirtz's form around
Sports.text:
Florian Wirtz says he is enjoying his best form yet at Liverpool and benefiting from Andoni Iraola's confidence and Jurgen Klopp's advice.

Wirtz, 23, scored in Liverpool's 4-0 win over Manchester United on Sunday and has three goals and six assists this season.

The Germany midfielder made the £116m move from Bayer Leverkusen in the summer of 2025 and after failing to make his mark in his first campaign in England, is beginning to showcase his quality for Iraola's side.

Speaking in Belgium before Liverpool's Champions League game against Club Brugge, Wirtz said: "I can't really say that I've changed that much.

"I've become a bit better on a physical level and that's the only reason that could explain it."

He also said he has been picking the brains of Germany manager Klopp, the former Liverpool boss, while on international duty.

"He tells me all the time that he loved his time here, the people love him here and tries to give me some advice to get successful over here as he has shown how it is done," Wirtz said.

"He can give me some good advice. It's always small things. More private things.

"But he is speaking good about the club, the region, the people, and that helps to hear someone who has experienced it for a long time."

Sports.title: F1 Q&A: Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc, Max Verstappen and George Russell feature
Sports.text:
After Las Vegas, have Ferrari now reached a crossroads? With Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc's on-track antics, is their partnership sustainable? Should Ferrari consider a change of direction, potentially bringing Oliver Bearman into the equation? - Michael

The battle between Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc at Ferrari is one that keeps on giving - but not in a way Ferrari would want.

The collision in Las Vegas for which Leclerc was penalised was just the latest flashpoint for the team in a season that has been full of them.

The drivers argued over race strategy in relation to each other in Zandvoort and Singapore.

Hamilton made an aggressive dive down the inside at the first chicane on the first lap at Monza, only for Leclerc to shove him on to the gravel.

Hamilton ignored calls to pit in both Singapore (because he didn't want to just circulate behind Leclerc) and Brazil (because, he said, he had not been given enough information about the weather).

There was the first-lap incident at Turn Four in Mexico in which their fighting led to both going off track and letting in Max Verstappen to win a race Ferrari should have finished one-two.

And now Las Vegas, where first Hamilton earned a 10-second penalty for gaining a position on Lando Norris on track in an incident that also involved Leclerc, then Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for tipping Hamilton into a spin later in the race.

Leclerc was on the receiving end of team principal Frederic Vasseur's ire in Las Vegas - the Frenchman calling the situation "unacceptable". But inside Ferrari they felt both drivers had a degree of culpability for the Mexico situation.

Somehow Vasseur needs to get a handle on this.

Ferrari want to allow them to race. And it's hard to imagine two drivers of such standing would accept anything else.

The problem is that doing so, amid their battle for supremacy within the team, is harming the team's results.

The concern for Ferrari is this is happening when there is relatively little at stake. It's easy to imagine how combustible it could become if Ferrari have a car capable of challenging for the title next year.

Both want to be the driver to deliver that next championship, for very different reasons.

Hamilton would get his eighth, which he feels he was unfairly denied in Abu Dhabi in 2021. And Leclerc would win his first, and complete the journey of being the first Ferrari academy driver to win the world championship for the team.

At the moment, this is not an existential question, but it's easy to see how it could become one, and Ferrari left with a decision of it being one or the other if they can't find a way to race without compromising the team.

But that's not just on Vasseur.

Both drivers have buy into that and, as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri have largely done at McLaren, accept there will be days when they have to sacrifice themselves for the greater good of Ferrari while ensuring they are ahead of the other more often than not on speed and fair racing.

It's then up to the team to decide when there comes a point to impose team orders if either or both are in a title fight with another driver.

It remains to be seen whether either of them can fully buy into that in circumstances when they individually end up losing out.

Why does George Russell often feel the need to try mind games and make comments, such as those about Max Verstappen? It often backfires on him and are usually made when he's got nothing to race for. Shouldn't he focus on himself? - Nick

This, as Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff pointed out after the race in Las Vegas, is a rivalry that goes back years.

"They've known each other so long," was Wolff's verdict. "Since karting. I think it's probably been a bit of cat and mouse. Provocations on either side. Another good factor of entertainment."

Verstappen also had a bit of a set-to with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in Mexico practice, which was not dissimilar in some ways.

There, stewards ruled that both had driven in an "unacceptable manner" and both drivers admitted their moves had been unnecessary and clumsy.

There's no question Russell believed what he was saying about Verstappen's driving in final practice at Las Vegas. According to the stewards, he was in the right, as Verstappen was given a warning for his changing direction in the braking zone.

Are these mind games? Or just Russell saying what he thinks? He feels he has a valid point to make.

Making it in public does not seem to affect Verstappen in any way. Does it change anything? Verstappen is a remorseless, ruthless competitor on track whether he is provoked or not.

Yes, he admitted satisfaction when he saw Russell make his late-race error in Las Vegas. But did he race any differently because of the Briton's comments? That's unlikely. Verstappen was just doing what he felt was right to win the race.

Ultimately, it's Russell's career, and it's up to him how he conducts himself, what he chooses to say in public and what he does not.

Track design, cold temperatures, energy deployment strategies or just the unwillingness of one team-mate to hold station behind another. What was the dominant factor in Las Vegas that led to such a hectic race? - Tim

The extraordinary Las Vegas race, with long trains of cars unable to break free of each other, was a combination of technical factors. Nothing to do with the willingness or otherwise of team-mates to hold station.

It was a combination of the track characteristics, particularly the long straights, the energy deployment demands of the engines, which are energy starved, and the cold temperatures and track surface and the effect they had on tyre behaviour.

As Max Verstappen said: "It was just the tow (in) combination with the deployment. Of course, when you are within a second, you have the overtake mode as well, and around here that is powerful. So, you could not pull away."

The tow provided a significant lap time gain of well over 0.5secs a lap. That's why a car in front could not pull away from a car behind even if it was slightly quicker.

The overtake mode provides an extra 0.5MJ of electrical energy per lap for a car following another by under a second. So that's another factor preventing someone pulling away.

Then the batteries were running out before the end of the straights, so a car running in front in free air was suffering from that, too.

On top of that, Las Vegas is a smooth track which is light on tyres. So degradation was almost non-existent. That kept tyre temperatures under control and allowed people to push hard throughout.

If the tyres had shown their usual behaviour of surface overheating leading to sliding, there would have been less action as drivers would have found it much harder to follow each other closely. As is usually the case in F1.

Drivers have been pushing for years for tyres to behave in this way, but so far Pirelli has been unable or unwilling to provide them. It only happens occasionally in specific circumstances.

The flip side of the argument is that so-called zero-deg races are sometimes boring as much as they are sometimes great, because drivers pushing to the limit can means less overtaking. Not in this case, though

With a move to engines with a smaller electrical component in 2030, are F1 cars becoming less relevant to modern road cars? The argument was always that F1 is the test bed for future road car technology. - Paul

The current F1 engines, with a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, were decided upon five or so years ago when the road-car market was slightly different to now.

The push for electrification is still there, and will continue. But consumer take-up of electric cars, especially in the performance market, has not been what manufacturers expected. Hence a slight shift in focus.

That said, it's not as if the current F1 engines are especially road relevant. With a few exceptions, road cars tend to be either full electric, plug-in hybrid, where the electrical element is much less than 50-50, or full internal combustion.

So there is an argument the new engines, with sustainable fuel and a hybrid element that is about 12-13% of total output normally or 25% when on overtake mode, are more relevant to road cars, not less, at least in their fundamental architecture.

The sustainable fuel is key here.

If this can get to a point where it is available to the mass market - and F1 is simplifying the demands on its make-up for the next ruleset in an attempt to help make the fuel more cost-effective for exactly that reason - it could be a game-changer for emissions in the road-car market.

That's because there will inevitably be a lot of legacy internal combustion vehicles on the road globally for many years, even after the new-car market becomes fully electric.

So if emissions from these can be reduced by 80%, as is the ballpark figure for the carbon-impact reduction of sustainable fuels versus fossil fuels, that's a major step.

Don't forget, too, the 2030 rules were the product of talks between the manufacturers and the FIA.

It was the manufacturers who pushed back against FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem's initial desire for a naturally aspirated engine with no hybrid element.

And they did that exactly because it made them more road relevant.

Gaming_Tech.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
Gaming_Tech.text:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations".

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Gaming_Tech.title: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
Gaming_Tech.text:
As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.

Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.

The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.

Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.

The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.

Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.

Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.

This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.

The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?

The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.

In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.

It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.

The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

Gaming_Tech.title: 'I'm proud of it': Killer confesses after murdering Ian Huntley
Gaming_Tech.text:
A triple murderer who beat the notorious child-killer Ian Huntley to death in prison has been given a second whole life jail term.

Anthony Russell, 44, repeatedly bludgeoned Huntley, 52, with a metal bar at the high security Frankland Prison near Durham in February, Newcastle Crown Court heard.

In footage released by the Crown Prosecution Service, Russell confesses to planning to kill Huntley and says: "I'm proud of it."

Russell, who was jailed for life with no chance of parole in March 2022 for raping and murdering a pregnant woman and killing a mother and son in the West Midlands, admitted Huntley's murder on the second day of his trial.

Sentencing him for what prosecutors called a "cold-blooded" and planned attack, Mr Justice Hilliard KC said Russell would never be freed from prison or eligible for parole.

Huntley was serving a life sentence at the high security Frankland jail for murdering Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in Soham, Cambridgeshire, in 2002.

Gaming_Tech.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
Gaming_Tech.text:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark trial in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which also included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said Huawei had grown into business with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff through hard work.

Following the verdict, Huawei said the five trade secret-related charges "were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades".

"No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation," the company said.

"We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests."

Gaming_Tech.title: Trump faces backlash after he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang
Gaming_Tech.text:
Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy.

The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

Trump said he "made the deal" with the tech giant's board to get Huang his job back, but both the president and Nvidia are facing backlash from lawmakers.

But his comeback added almost $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value as its share price jumped 31%, ending ended a streak of losses on the US stock market.

Nvidia's gains helped boost shares in other tech companies and financial markets in Asia while European markets were flat.

However, despite Huang's return, Nvidia's share price remains down over the past month amid investor concerns about the wider AI industry and future development.

But it is a dramatic return for the man dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" to the company at the centre of the AI spending boom.

Attention will soon turn to Huang's appearance before Congress next week, where the Nvidia boss will be questioned over his relationship with Alice Huang, alleged to be a spy for China, due to national security concerns.

On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang (no relation) was chief executive. China has denied the spying allegations.

Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's reinstatement after originally resigning on 12 November was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Last Tuesday, the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him following calls to do so and Huang himself stating he would be open to returning.

The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after...

Gaming_Tech.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.

That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.

The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.

Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.

While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.

The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.

Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.

It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?

That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.

Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".

Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
