BreakingNewsTab.title: Former Civil Nuclear Constabulary chief inspector jailed for rape
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A former police chief inspector who once worked with convicted murderer Wayne Couzens has been sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for two counts of rape and one of sexual assault.

Glen Mahony, 54, who was convicted at Maidstone Crown Court in September following a 10-day trial, carried out two attacks while his victim was asleep.

Mahony worked in the Civil Nuclear Constabulary (CNC) and previously worked with Couzens, who is serving a whole life tariff for the rape and murder of Sarah Everard in 2021.

In his sentencing remarks on Tuesday, Judge Gareth Branston dismissed Mahony's claims that he was targeted because he had once managed Couzens.

"You were not targeted. You were arrested because of what you did," he said.

He described Mahony's behaviour as "appalling", saying it had left his victim, who was known to him, suffering panic attacks and unable to work.

The judge said that when arrested in March 2022, Mahony told Kent Police officers that he had been Wayne Couzens's overall manager, though not his line manager.

The CNC, which guards the UK's nuclear facilities, is the force where Couzens served for six years before joining the Metropolitan Police.

Mahony, who was an inspector in charge of day-to-day police operations at the Dungeness power station before being promoted, was his commanding officer for some of that time.

Mahony was suspended on full pay by the CNC in March 2022 and resigned the day before a disciplinary hearing in January of this year.

The CNC said he would have been dismissed for gross misconduct if the disciplinary process had been carried out.

In an impact statement read to the court, his victim said she was made to feel worthless, and that "it was all about control for him".

"His actions didn't just hurt me at the time but have continued to do so each day. He has stolen my confidence," she said, having described ongoing nightmares and mental health struggles.

Det Ch Insp Tracy Evans, of Kent Police, said: "To take advantage of a woman while she is asleep and at her most vulnerable is utterly disgraceful and to then deny it happened and force the victim to relive her ordeal during a trial makes things even worse."

She also praised the "tremendous courage" of the victim in coming forward to report Mahony.

CNC Chief Constable Simon Chesterman said his immediate thoughts were with Mahony's victim, who he also commended for her bravery.

"Former officer Glen Mahony's crimes were despicable, committing the most serious sexual violence to a vulnerable female victim, who was not able to consent," he said.

"Mahony's behaviours are entirely contrary to the high standards required of a police officer with the CNC. And his actions go on to undermine the trust and confidence that the public, and particularly women, have in the police service."

Two WhatsApp groups to which Mahony belonged were also investigated by CNC professional standards.

"In these groups, Mahony sent sexist and misogynistic messages, and he did not challenge or leave the group when others sent similarly offensive messages," Chief Constable Chesterman said.

"This further underlines his disgusting opinion of women."

Mahony was promoted to chief inspector for the south division in 2020. It meant he was number three in the division's chain of command for the four nuclear sites in the south - Dungeness, Sizewell and Hinkley Point power stations, and the nuclear research centre at Harwell, Oxfordshire.

He spent most of his working life as an armed officer based at the Dungeness nuclear plant in Kent.

He joined the force in 2006, becoming a sergeant in 2011 before being promoted to inspector in 2016. This put him in operational charge of security at the site. He would have worked with Couzens, who was a constable at Dungeness between 2012 and 2018.

Couzens was also in a separate WhatsApp group with six other officers who transferred to the Met from the CNC. The messages they shared were found to be sexist, misogynistic, racist and violent, raising questions about the culture among officers at both the CNC and the Met.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Andy Burnham has been accused of turning the UK into "a joke" on the world stage by Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, amid a row about social media videos posted from an event in Downing Street.

Social media influencer Max Balegde has deleted a video filmed outside the door of Number 10, which was posted on TikTok, in which he mimed along to explicit lyrics.

Badenoch said it was a "disgrace" that the prime minister allowed 10 Downing Street to be "degraded".

The prime minister's spokesperson said the content was clearly not acceptable and it was "right" that Balegde had taken down the social media posts.

Balegde's video appears to have been filmed earlier this month at an event for around 60 social media influencers hosted by Burnham, who is eager to use social media to reach younger voters. Balegde also gave a speech to those present at the event.

In the video, the influencer, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

Bomboclaat is a Jamaican profanity referring to a menstrual cloth, while pussy is a slang term for female genitals.

It is unclear when Balegde's video was deleted but it no longer appears on his TikTok or Instagram accounts.

The creator has 3.6 million followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram.

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones, the BBC can reveal.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

One of the distinctive features of Burnham's time in office has been his enthusiasm for engaging with social media influencers as a means to communicate with different groups of voters, especially younger voters.

It was an approach begun by Sir Keir Starmer, under whom a "new media unit" was formed, but has significantly intensified since July.

The engagement with influencers has elicited criticism of Burnham from those who fear it means reduced scrutiny and diminished opportunities to hold the prime minister to account.

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Badenoch said she had been "pretty shocked" by the videos coming out of the event, questioning whether they were in good taste.

She said that while Burnham might think he was connecting with young people, many people around the world "will think our country is a joke".

She said: "I do think Andy Burnham should apologise for the way he is using Number 10 as his personal studio to carry out these silly TikToks.

"Vladimir Putin, President Xi and all sorts of other people who are hostile to the UK will see these things, they will get reports of them, and they will see that our prime minister is not a serious man and they will think we are not a serious country."

In a reference to Balegde's video, she said: "I think it is a disgrace that Number 10 – that door which is a symbol of British democracy, power and authority in the world, dignity, that's where we receive people like President Zelensky, showing them that they have the support of people in this country, is being degraded in this way."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage also criticised the use of the Downing Street door as "puerile" and "demeaning" but said he wouldn't ban influencers from Number 10.

"I wouldn't let them behave quite the way that it happened," he said.

"It showed a slight lack of respect for the place and for the office and was really very inappropriate indeed."

Responding to questions about Balegde's video, the prime minister's spokesperson said "the content was clearly not acceptable", but added "content creators are responsible for what they choose to post".

Asked repeatedly whether Number 10 had requested for the video be removed, the spokesperson said: "It is right the creator took down that content.

"It's clearly not acceptable and that is reflected by the fact that it has been taken down."

They also defended the decision to invite influencers to Downing Street, saying it was "right that the PM listens to" social media content creators who "reach millions of people who don't get their news from traditional media".

Balegde also gave a speech inside the influencers' event, which was held by Burnham in an attempt to build links with a growing sector of the economy.

A smaller group of creators were asked to arrive early to film videos with the prime minister.

One attendee in this group said they had to run ideas past the prime minister's team for approval.

A government spokesperson said they would not comment on security and whether the footage captured on the government phones was reviewed, but said it was "not abnormal" for attendees of Downing Street to use government phones.

BreakingNewsTab.title: French ex-President Nicolas Sarkozy and wife Carla Bruni to be tried next year
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Nicolas Sarkozy and his wife Carla Bruni-Sarkozy are to face trial next year over charges stemming from the former French president's conviction for conspiring to fund his election campaign with money from late Libyan dictator Muammar Gaddafi.

The charges centre on the retraction of the testimony of a key witness who had initially said he had evidence that could incriminate Sarkozy.

The pair deny any wrongdoing.

Sarkozy was given a five-year sentence in the case last September and became the first French ex-president to go to jail, even though he only spent 20 days behind bars. He has always denied doing anything wrong in the case and the appeals verdict is expected next Monday.

Since losing his re-election bid in 2012, Sarkozy has faced several criminal investigations.

In 2024, he was handed a one-year sentence – of which six months were suspended – over the illegal financing of his 2012 re-election campaign.

In 2021, he was found guilty of trying to bribe a judge and sentenced to three years in jail – two of them suspended – and thus became the first former French president to get a custodial sentence. He was allowed to serve his time at home wearing a tag instead of going to jail.

The new case centres on a Libyan businessman, Ziad Takieddine, who had said he had written proof that Sarkozy's 2007 campaign bid was "abundantly" financed by Tripoli, and that the €50m (£43m) in payments continued after he became president.

Takieddine, who died last year, withdrew his accusations in an interview in 2020.

At the time, Sarkozy was said to have stated: the "truth is finally coming out", but officials found the retraction to be "insincere" and a new investigation was launched into the "Save Sarko" file – the nickname the alleged perpetrators had used for the operation, according to French media.

So the former head of state and his wife, an Italian-born former supermodel and singer, will now face charges of "criminal conspiracy with intent to commit fraud" and benefiting from witness tampering. They deny any wrongdoing.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Saurav Das CJP: Indian government has 'lost the plot' says 'cockroach' party leader after being barred from UK flight
BreakingNewsTab.text:
One of the leaders of India's "cockroach" movement has said the Delhi government has "completely lost the plot" after he was stopped from leaving the country for the UK.

Saurav Das said he was meant to board a flight on Tuesday morning but was told by immigration officers his passport had been "flagged" because of discrepancies involving his date of birth.

In an interview with the BBC, Das said there were no discrepancies in his documents, accusing the Indian government of using cheap tactics to stop activists from travelling and speaking on issues that matter to young people.

The BBC has reached out to the federal home ministry, Delhi police and airport officials for comment.

Saurav told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme the incident showed the government was "scared".

"They are scared of the cockroach movement. They're scared of young people asking them questions because they have never had to deal with a generation that wants to ask questions so head on. So that jitters them."

By not allowing him to travel, he said the government had lowered India's stature in the world.

"It's international news that I am unable to travel to the UK," he said. "And this shows Prime Minister Modi in such poor light.

"It's a way to harass, to target activists, young voices in India by the Modi government."

Das said he had been invited by the Oxford Union, as well as universities including Cambridge and Edinburgh, to speak about the movement.

Ratna Singh, another leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), wrote: "The manner in which Saurav was not allowed to board today raises deeply troubling questions about the state of freedom of expression and the space being allowed for young voices in this country."

On Tuesday, the London School of Economics Student Union's Amnesty International Unit, a student-led charity group, shared a post on Instagram saying that an event featuring Das had been "indefinitely postponed".

Das, a former journalist, became one of the faces of the CJP - a Gen Z-led movement that began as satire but has since emerged as a youth-led pressure group.

In July, protests spearheaded by the CJP over exam paper leaks led to the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan .

In October, CJP leaders including Das were among thousands detained by the police for trying to hold protests demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing.

The same month, Das and Ashutosh Ranka, another CJP leader, were jailed for seven days after being arrested for trespassing at a banned protest site in Delhi.

Das insisted the CJP would continue protesting, but it did not want to be a political party "as of today".

"It's a long haul. We are not here for a short time. We are looking at India in the next 10 to 20 years. How do we develop India into a better country? That is the vision that we want to carry forward."

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of CJP, wrote on X that if Das "had looted a bank or committed financial fraud", he may have been allowed to fly to London, referring to billionaire bank-loan defaulters who have left India.

There have been other instances in recent years of people being prevented from boarding flights.

In September 2025, Bhanu Tatak, an environmental and anti-dam activist from India's north-eastern Arunachal Pradesh state, was stopped from boarding a flight to Dublin.

In March 2022, Rana Ayyub, an investigative journalist and outspoken critic of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government, was also stopped from boarding a flight to London at the Mumbai airport. She was due to speak at different events on media freedom and the targeting of journalists.

Additional reporting by Cherylann Mollan.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Syria land mine casualties soar, two years after war
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Eleven-year-old Alaa was tending her family's goats with her siblings in a field behind their home in Umm Khuzaym, north-west Syria, on Sunday when there was a flash and a deafening bang.

"Then we heard people screaming," Alaa's father, Walid Mohammed Al-Ghafar, told the BBC.

Walid ran outside to find his daughter lying face down, killed, and her 10-year-old brother, Mahmoud, seriously injured.

Unwittingly, the children had triggered a landmine.

The incident and others this week bring to nearly 1,000 the number of children killed or injured by explosive ordnance in Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, according to the UN Mine Action Service (Unmas).

The village is one of many where families have returned to homes and farmland that were once on the front lines of Syria's 13-year civil war.

Alaa's father said demining teams had visited several times to clear the fields. He and other residents believed it was safe for farmers and children to move around.

But mines and other explosives can lie far beyond former battle lines, making it difficult to establish which areas are safe.

"Remnants of war from today's conflicts are often very widely and broadly scattered, often without patterns, which makes it extremely difficult to do clearance," Katrin Atkins, research lead at Landmine Monitor, a global mine monitoring initiative, told the BBC.

The dangers are reflected in a sharp rise in casualties across Syria.

A total of 1,602 people were killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war in 2025 alone, an increase of more than 50% on the previous year, according to the Landmine Monitor report, published by the International Campaign to Ban Landmines on Tuesday.

Only Myanmar, with 1,891 casualties, recorded more.

The report attributes the rise in Syria partly to the large-scale return of refugees and internally displaced people following Assad's overthrow.

"When you look at population movement, a couple of months later you see an increase of incidents in these areas, because that's exactly where people go and start to use the fields again," Atkins said.

More than 60% of casualties recorded by the world's largest landmine clearance charity, the Halo Trust, involve farming, agriculture or shepherding, according to its Syria programme manager, Simon Jackson.

"They're not going to wait for the government or for organisations like us to come and tell them that everything is safe and clear," he told the BBC. "People are taking risks out of desperation."

Since Assad's fall on 8 December 2024, Unmas has recorded at least 1,556 incidents in Syria involving explosive ordnance.

They have caused 2,701 casualties: 935 people killed and 1,766 injured. Children account for 995 of those victims, or about 37%.

But the toll is likely to be higher, with experts estimating that overall casualties could be under-reported by 25-50%.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Emir of Daura: Nigerian monarch suspended over sexual assault claims
BreakingNewsTab.text:
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

She posted a video, which has since been deleted, in which a man who appears to be the emir is holding her hands in his lap.

After some moments she was heard saying: "Stop, stop" as the hands reached for her chest.

According to a statement, Katsina Governor Dikko Umaru Radda directed the immediate constitution of a committee to investigate the allegations.

The statement said the state government was taking the allegations seriously and would rely on the committee's findings to determine the appropriate course of action.

It said the committee's findings and recommendations would be fully implemented, stressing that justice would be served.

However, it did not disclose the membership of the investigative committee, its terms of reference or the timeline for submitting its report.

The emir has been on the throne since 2007, succeeding his brother Bashar dan Umaru, who reigned for 41 years.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Israeli air strike kills Hamas internal security chief in Gaza
BreakingNewsTab.text:
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.

Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.

The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.

Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.

Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.

The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.

Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.

Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.

The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".

It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".

Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.

Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.

Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

FinanceTab.title: Will I get the £100 energy payment and when will I receive it?
FinanceTab.text:
Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment to help with their energy bills this winter, Chancellor John Healey has announced in his Budget.

Here's what you need to know about the payment.

For many people, the £100 on offer is a lot of money, but it's worth considering the context.

A typical energy bill is forecast to jump by £443 a year from January, according to consultants Cornwall Insight.

Therefore many people will still feel worse off despite the payment.

Those living in properties which are in council tax bands A to D in England will get the payment, the government has said.

As such, it's worth checking which council tax band your home is in, external. If you live in England, you can use the search function by typing your postcode into the box.

If you get a paper council tax bill, your band will also be printed on there.

The chancellor said the policy was for England but that funding would be given to Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland to make the payment as well.

The Scottish and Welsh governments have confirmed they will use the funding to introduce equivalent or similar payment schemes.

The Northern Irish government does not have the legal authority to make the £100 payments unless it agrees its budget, which it has failed to do since the start of this financial year.

If you pay your council tax by direct debit, the money will be paid directly into your bank account.

Those who don't pay by direct debit will be contacted by their council and given the choice to receive the £100 directly into their bank account or as credit on their council tax bill.

The government will ask councils to make payments from 4 January, and the scheme will be open until the end of May.

Students living in halls will not get the payment because student halls are not in council tax bands A to D.

However, if you're a student living in a property that is in council tax bands A to D, as in a private home or flat let out by a landlord, then you will get the payment.

Students do not pay council tax so the local authority will be responsible for finding a way to give them the payments.

This is also the case for those who do not pay council tax because of another kind of exemption, or if you do pay council tax but you do it by cash or some other way.

The government said it would give councils guidance on how local authorities should do this in due course.

FinanceTab.title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
FinanceTab.text:
Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load".

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

FinanceTab.title: The shake-up facing renters as a new kind of landlord emerges
FinanceTab.text:
On Christmas Eve 2021, there was a knock on the door of Lexi Levens' rented flat. It was a letter sent by special delivery from the NHS nurse's landlord saying she, her husband, and four children had two months to move out.

"The kids all thought it was a present arriving," she recalls.

Lexi's landlord had used something known then as a Section 21 notice to evict her family without needing to give a reason.

Lexi, along with the housing charity Shelter, went on to lobby the government to improve rights for renters. The Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May this year, banned Section 21 evictions and also made it illegal to refuse to rent to people based on their status as a family with children.

The landlords Lexi had been renting from at that time were typical of the English housing market - individuals who owned one or a handful of properties.

Many of these small landlords say the Renters' Rights Act has left them feeling squeezed. They also say rising interest rates, new regulations and tax changes (including some in the most recent Budget) are making things harder. Some say they are selling up.

Meanwhile, according to Savills estate agents, 2026 is likely to be another record year for investment from large institutions in what is known in the property industry as build to rent (BTR). This is when big developers build blocks of flats or family housing to rent out, something that is commonplace in parts of Europe and the US. It means that rather than dealing with an individual landlord or letting agent, tenants are instead renting from larger, typically corporate, entities.

So does the shift, as some believe, represent a welcome professionalisation of the UK rental sector? Or will renters increasingly miss the positive elements of the personal touch that small landlords can provide?

According to the latest government survey of private landlords in England, 83% of English landlords own four properties or fewer, representing 51% of tenancies.

And according to 2024 research by real estate agency Savills, around 40% rental homes in the US and Germany are owned by large institutions - be they private firms, listed companies, pension funds, or co-operatives. For the UK, Savills calculated that figure was just 3%.

But the rental market is changing. The trend is most visible in England, where BTR has boomed in large cities and where regulations like the Renters' Rights Act apply, but there are BTR developments in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland too and the devolved nations are also seeing increased regulation on landlords, such as with Scotland's rent controls.

Lexi is pleased with the idea of a sector with stricter rules for landlords and more professional institutions getting involved.

"Anything that takes away from landlords having personal preferences [around choosing who they are or not prepared to rent to]… is a good thing," she says, adding that she believes large, corporate landlords would be less likely to act that way.

Not everyone is convinced BTR landlords are better, though.

Clint Stevenson, a 44-year-old magician for weddings and events, has been renting his one-bedroom flat in Ramsgate for £550 a month for two years. He says he has "the most amazing landlady" - an older woman who he regularly chats to. He sometimes walks her dog and does her shopping as well.

He says he had considered renting from a BTR development, but found the accommodation to be "very industrial and very unpersonal". He also found what was on offer to be expensive compared to what he is used to paying.

"They just look like big, money-grabbing deals," he says.

In Cardiff, Grainger, the UK's largest listed BTR developer, is currently offering a fully-furnished studio flat on the 20th floor of The Copper Works in the city centre with views over the bay for £1,265 a month.

It's a lot more than what is currently on offer on Rightmove, a 15 minute walk away from the city centre - a fully-furnished, ground-floor, one-bedroom flat with a garden for £800 a month.

But tenants in The Copper Works have free access to a gym, a cinema room, a roof terrace, and a games room. There's also free WiFi, a concierge service with a helpline, and other amenities. In addition, the studio flat has an EPC B rating as opposed to an EPC C rating for the one-bedroom flat down the road.

"You have to look at what you're getting for your rent," says Helen Gordon, Grainger's chief executive. She says BTR landlords can offer these services because of their scale. As she puts it: "If you run 11,000 homes, you can afford to invest in systems, processes, people, helplines – that sort of thing – that smaller landlords can't."

Gordon strongly pushes back against suggestions that there is a lack of human connection within BTR, noting that tenants are able to speak with staff whenever they need and that the firm regularly organises events for socialising with other tenants to create a sense of community.

It's a pattern across the BTR sector: a higher price point in exchange for what is marketed as high-quality accommodation and a suite of services - some in the sector even refer to 'customers' rather than 'tenants'.

The number of BTR homes has tripled between 2019 and 2025, and while it represents just 3% of the overall rental market at the moment, Gordon believes it could reach "at least 10%" over the next ten years. "And I think it could go higher," she adds.

"If you've got major institutions that include pension funds, financial institutions, and FTSE 250 companies running the stock, it's easier to hold people to account than lots of disparate people, so you can see why it's attractive [to government]."

A 2012 government-commissioned report concluded that more BTR properties could help increase housing supply and drive economic growth as well as providing tenants with more choice and better quality housing. It recommended central government and councils support the development of BTR through favourable planning decisions and releasing public land.

There is a lot of evidence governments and local authorities listened. Local leaders in big cities – London and Manchester, in particular – have partnered with developers to deliver large housing projects involving, in many cases, the release of public land. Kings Cross in London is a prime example of this and current London Mayor Sadiq Khan's push for BTR development near Transport for London (TFL) land, mostly Tube stations, is another example. As part of that, TfL formed a joint venture with Grainger.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, says it's not a matter of looking at one policy, government, or council in particular but more the "policy environment" which has been around since the 2010s.

He points to a series of tax changes, including mortgage interest tax relief changes and higher stamp duty rates for second homes and buy-to-let properties introduced by the Conservatives around 10 years ago, which made the sector less favourable for smaller landlords.

The Renters' Rights Act and more stringent energy efficiency requirements were later introduced. And the last two Budgets have raised taxes on rental income from next year. The tax change applies to individuals who are landlords, not to BTR companies which pay corporation tax, further encouraging professionalisation of the sector.

Yet, while many welcome these changes, others say they are pushing smaller landlords out of the sector. As Cook puts it, there has been more "stick" for small landlords than "carrot" for the BTR sector.

Between 2000 and 2016, a net 2.74 million homes were added to the English rental market in total, according to an analysis of government data by the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. In the 10 years since, a net of just 200,000 have. For renters, it is now less likely that your property is owned by a smaller landlord.

Kevin Barber started off with one rental home. He has since grown this portfolio to 40 properties with his business partner but resents what he sees as the clout of the BTR sector. "The big property companies have got so much financial power and influence with the government," he says.

But whether we will actually see more homes being built is another matter. Savills' Cook says BTR development could slow in future as high interest rates and increased building costs continue to hit developers' bottom line. These same factors are why housebuilders say they are building less.

Cook says the current rate of BTR development won't be enough to meet the demand for rental properties on its own, at least not imminently. In addition, while some BTR developers do build cheaper family homes for rent in the suburbs, the sector is largely still building blocks of flats for wealthier renters living in cities.

This raises the possibility that the UK could end up with a two-tier rental market – what Cook describes as the "haves and the have nots" – where high-earning city-dwelling renters have their pick of rental properties but poorer renters in suburbs struggle to find somewhere to live.

Unless the government steps in, possibly by delivering more housing itself or partnering with developers to do so, it might find any positives gained by the Renters' Rights Act are undone by an increasingly fragmented rental market.

FinanceTab.title: BBC exposes Whitby dog breeder selling sick puppies for £2k each
FinanceTab.text:
When Katie Thornton paid £2,000 for a nine-week-old puppy for her son, she knew it was a premium price - but was happy to be doing business with a "legit", council-approved breeder.

But Ozzy the Dobermann pup started coughing in the car on the way home, and within 48 hours he was in a veterinary hospital receiving urgent treatment for pneumonia.

Since then, his ongoing health problems mean Katie has racked up more than £5,000 in vet bills.

A BBC investigation has found the breeder had been stripped of his five-star rating two months before selling several sick puppies, but continued to advertise as five-star.

We have also found at least 15 other breeders in England advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than it really is.

An expert reviewing our findings - including undercover footage we recorded at the breeder's home - said the investigation exposes a nationwide "wild west" of dog licensing, making it "easy for consumers to be scammed".

The breeder has not responded to our request for comment.

When Katie visited the premises of Mikjulora Dobermanns in Whitby, North Yorkshire, she said the puppies' mother "didn't look very well" and was "skinny" and "shaking".

But she felt the breeder, Michael Estill, was "pushing me to buy Ozzy" so she paid for him and took him home on the spot.

Katie defended her decision because she had done extensive research to check the business was "legit".

The mother-of-one, from Harrogate, said she had checked his licence number and read through his website and online adverts, which said he had decades of experience and a "five-star" breeding licence.

In England, local councils grant breeders in their area a licence and star rating dependent on welfare standards.

Vet reports for North Yorkshire Council from August and December 2025, seen by the BBC, cited dozens of concerns with Estill's business, including:

"Poor" living conditions "akin to a prison", with dogs kept in cages, stacked on top of each other, that were too small for them to turn around in

Deteriorating health and welfare of "sad" dogs

Puppies for sale not matching descriptions - "in other words it is a scam"

Prospective buyers "very vulnerable to unsuspectingly purchasing unhealthy puppies"

The business was "more or less a puppy farm masquerading as an honest and conscientious breeder. This must stop"

Estill "bullied" a local vet to perform an "unnecessary" Caesarean section on one of his dogs, to reduce the time he would have to spend monitoring her

His "demanding" behaviour led the practice to give him several doses of a powerful stimulant which he gave to one of his dogs at home - which the vet considered to be "negligent"

He had a three-year-old dog euthanised because he suspected her to have a neurological condition, despite the vet encouraging him to get diagnostic tests and specialist treatment first.

Following the reports, which concluded that the business was "functioning outside the law", the council renewed Estill's licence in January but downgraded his rating from five-star (the highest standards) to one-star (minor failings).

Dr Caroline Allen, founder of Pet Lighthouse and former RSPCA chief veterinary officer, said she was "surprised and shocked" that the business kept its licence.

A North Yorkshire Council spokesperson said the threshold for revoking a licence "was not considered to have been met on the evidence available".

They added: "We take animal welfare very seriously and investigate concerns brought to our attention.

"Following the veterinary inspection reports, we have continued to work with the licence holder to address the identified concerns and are satisfied that standards have significantly improved, resulting in a higher level of animal welfare at the premises."

The BBC has evidence that Estill continued to sell puppies while claiming on his website and in person that he was five-star rated.

While Estill has since updated his website homepage, he has not updated the metadata, which means when his business is searched for online the five-star claim still appears alongside a link to his site.

There is no official list of licensed breeders and their star ratings, and not all councils publish them, so Katie took his word for it.

"If I would've known he was a one-star breeder, I would've never even gone to the property. I wouldn't have bought a dog off a one-star breeder," she said, adding that she wanted to see Estill's licence revoked.

Kat Durrant's dog Bentley died aged three in 2022 of a heart condition known as dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM).

Within days of bringing him home from Mikjulora Dobermanns, Kat says Bentley was "really poorly".

"The vet asked me if I had got the dog from a puppy farm because of his condition," she added.

Three years later, Kat had Bentley put to sleep as his weak heart was "giving up" and he was struggling to breathe.

"Bentley suffered his whole life because of everything he'd been through when he was young," she said.

Kat, from Manchester, set up a Facebook group where other people who had bought dogs from Estill could share their experiences.

Including Kat, owners of 17 dogs mentioned in the group said the pets had died before the age of eight, including 10 below the age of four.

Several others claimed their dogs were sick at a young age but survived.

The vet report from December 2025 said Estill was not correctly testing his dogs for DCM despite his website saying that he did test.

The report said the fact that Estill did "nothing" when customers told him about DCM diagnoses was "truly the hallmark of a breeder who does not care about the welfare or improving the breed".

Michelle Paton, who lives in Edinburgh, bought her puppy Cruz a week before Katie bought Ozzy.

He had a cough "as soon as he came through the front door" and was diagnosed with pneumonia and possible heart failure a few weeks later.

Michelle was frustrated to discover Kat's Facebook group and felt Estill's licence should have been revoked "years ago".

"If somebody was actually doing their job properly then they would have put an end to him breeding a long time ago," she said.

Caroline Housam, from York, bought her puppy Roxy the day before Katie bought Ozzy.

Roxy started coughing in the car on the journey home.

When Caroline took Roxy to the vet she said she was told there were problems with her glands, and later they found she had a limp and ulcers in her eyes.

She is having ongoing treatment and tests.

"I'm actually angry because I look at my dog and I'm thinking, 'I don't know what lies ahead'," said Caroline.

"When you listen to what other people have said [on Facebook] who have had [dogs] bred from him, her chances of living until two are slim."

BBC research has found at least 15 other breeders in England who are also advertising puppies alongside claims their star rating is higher than the one they have been given by their local authority.

We checked through a list of 806 breeders with a rating between one and four stars.

Of the 573 breeders rated three-star or below (meaning lower standards), we could not find mention of a rating on their websites, social media pages or in online adverts for puppies in 541 cases.

Of the 32 who did mention a rating, 11 had active adverts claiming to be more highly rated than they really were.

Of the 45 four-star rated breeders to mention a rating, four claimed they were five-star in active adverts.

One council confirmed a breeder we enquired about did not have a licence at all, another said they could not find the information we needed, and others took weeks to respond.

The list of breeders was provided by Paws on the Doors, an organisation aiming to collate breeders' star ratings across the country in one place. For each of the breeders whose online claims did not match the Paws on the Doors list, we checked with individual councils to verify the up-to-date rating.

Commenting on the BBC's findings, Paws on the Doors co-founder Leigh Grant said the main reason "the scammers exist" was that central government and local councils had "failed" to properly implement the principles of legislation for breeder licensing from 2018.

He said a lack of support for animal welfare had led to a position where breeders can "falsely claim higher standards, without fear of detection".

Allen said our findings showed puppy breeding was "an absolute wild west" and there should be "countrywide teams of inspectors and vets who are properly trained to understand the legislation".

She said: "It is easy for consumers to be scammed, but unfortunately at the heart of this there are really vulnerable animals and puppies."

Amy Thompson-Copsey, senior public affairs officer at Dogs Trust, said potential puppy owners should "trust your instinct" to avoid falling for "financial scams".

"If something seems off, if you feel red flags, just walk away. You don't know what you could be getting into."

A Defra spokesperson said they were committed to ending "low welfare dog breeding" and were consulting on reforms to protect dogs' health and better inform the public on "which breeders they can trust".

The BBC put all allegations to Michael Estill and his wife Julie Estill, who is the named director of Mikjulora on Companies House, but they did not respond.

Additional data journalism by Anil Kumar Bharath.

FinanceTab.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
FinanceTab.text:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

FinanceTab.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologizes to staff: ‘I made some terrible mistakes’
FinanceTab.text:
Jensen Huang apologized to staff on Tuesday for the tumult he’s caused at Nvidia. The company’s CEO acknowledged he violated the code of conduct for having extramarital affairs, but pushed back on the reports that Donald Trump was instrumental in his reinstatement as chief executive.

“I made some terrible mistakes,” he said, according to a livestream reviewed by the New York Times. “I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids and, of course, I hurt all of you.”

The apology came one day after Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, and less than two weeks after he was ousted from the role. Following a whiplash series of events, the company’s board of directors reinstated Huang on Monday, despite his admission that he’d had an affair. News reports allege the CEO had romantic relationships with two company employees and a suspected Chinese spy.

During Tuesday’s apology, Huang told staffers he was in therapy and that it was “not acceptable” that he violated the company’s code of conduct. In an impromptu speech to employees on Monday, Huang said he was “terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this” and that he’s “going to be a better CEO the second time around”.

While Huang apologized for his affairs, he rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, according to the New York Times. He added that it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him. The board changed course, he said, because it “evaluated the entire situation” and “gathered facts”. Huang said Trump assured the board that he was not a national security threat.

The US government has been investigating whether Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged ex-lover, Alice Huang (no relation), diverted Nvidia semiconductors to China in breach of export controls. US government officials have also raised concerns about Alice Huang’s alleged role as a Chinese asset.

Trump reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return, according to Semafor. Nvidia’s board publicly said on Monday that it reached its decision to bring back Huang with “input from senior levels of the United States government”.

Huang potentially faces two congressional hearings next week, one before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and one before the Senate Banking committee. Gregory Meeks, a democratic congressman from New York and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said on Tuesday that despite Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia’s CEO, a hearing should still take place.

“The American people deserve to hear publicly from Mr Huang about how potentially billions of dollars’ worth of our most advanced technology wound up in the hands of our greatest competitor, and what role this administration played,” Meeks said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to request for comment.

FinanceTab.title: US school bus drivers decline amid low pay and poor work conditions
FinanceTab.text:
The number of school bus drivers in the US has dropped 5% over the last year as drivers continue to experience low pay, poor working conditions and school budget shortfalls, according to a new report.

The total number of school bus drivers is down 15%, or nearly 34,000 drivers, compared with 2019 levels, according to an new analysis from the Economic Policy Institute.

The 5% decrease from 2025 to 2026 represents a loss of nearly 10,200 drivers and was the largest single-year decline since 2022 for a workforce that transports an estimated 26 million children daily, the largest mass transit program in the US.

Dawn Freedenburg, who has been a school bus driver for 16 years in Chicago, Illinois, said the long process to be trained and licensed to be a school bus driver can deter new drivers. New drivers must get the proper commercial drivers license (CDL) and undergo extensive training and background checks to do the job, a process which requires weeks of unpaid work.

“It isn’t easy for most people to put that much time into a new job without being paid, especially in this economy,” said Freedenburg.

And once they get the job, wages typically range from $19 to $27 an hour, but most drivers don’t average 40 hours per week during the school year and receive no pay during school breaks. Few contractors or school districts provide additional benefits such as health insurance, she added.

“My current district guarantees five hours per day for 174 school days a year, but our work can fall anywhere between 5.45am and 5pm depending on your route assignments,” she added. “There is the possibility of extra work like field trips sometimes, but there are typically more drivers wanting them then trips available.”

The decline and ongoing shortages of school bus drivers have often forced school districts to cut and consolidate bus routes. Eighty-percent of school districts in the US have been affected by bus driver shortages, with 73% experiencing shortages from budget shortfalls, according to a 2025 report from the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

Higher diesel costs amid the war with Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine have worsened budget issues, costing school districts an estimated $1.1bn more from November 2025 to October 2026 compared to the previous year.

Wages for school bus drivers also dropped in September 2026 by 0.7% from September 2025 after accounting for inflation, while pay for other bus drivers has remained steady. Median hourly pay for school bus drivers was $22.49 in 2026, compared to a median hourly pay of $23.89 for all bus drivers. School bus drivers comprise 39.4% of all bus drivers.

Drivers also say that student behavior has also worsened since the Covid-19 pandemic, and school bus drivers are often caught in between the administration and parents, making it difficult to address behavioral issues.

Peter Sandler began working as a school bus driver in 2020 in Connecticut after retiring in 2016, noting that many bus drivers are retirees, which contributes to high turnover rates of school bus drivers.

As a result of bus driver shortages, his former contractor consolidated bus routes and increased the number of children per bus.

“That made buses filled to capacity which makes the driver’s life a nightmare,” Sandler said. “Every parent should be forced to see how their children act when they ride the school bus.”

Sandler also noted that with only 5.5 hours of paid work a day and little work when school is out of session, it is economically unfeasible to make ends meet as a school bus driver.

“If you add in summer work and taking charter work, its difficult to get past $40,000 annually,” he added. “Obviously, that’s not a lot of money, especially in a region where a one bedroom apartment would set you back $1,600 to $1,700 a month in the cheapest communities, and over $2,000 a month in better areas.”

Antonia Namnath, a school bus driver in the Beaverton school district in Oregon explained the school bus driver shortage isn’t an issue in her school district because the drivers are paid good wages, with starting wages ranging from $26 to $33 an hour, with annual increases tied to a union contract with the Oregon School Employees Association (OSEA Chapter 48).

“We get a good wage, incredible benefits, health benefits, vision, dental, everything,” she noted.

“The drivers have to be greatly compensated for the responsibility they’re taking on, which is to transport children safely from point A to point B, and manage the students in a safe way.”

Melissa Fay France, a school bus driver outside of Kalamazoo, Michigan, said the lack of medical insurance and low pay often make leaving the profession an attractive option for drivers.

With the “responsibility there is being a driver and maintaining your CDL, those wages need to match that,” France said. “I am a great driver, both on the road and for the kids. I know my worth and the schools aren’t living up to their end.”

FinanceTab.title: Tech sell-off resumes as euphoria from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return subsides
FinanceTab.text:
Technology shares led a market retreat Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s extraordinary return to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide.

A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30%, adding more than $900bn to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 9% mid-session.

Anthropic also slumped, giving up about 12% to $77.19, below its $83 price for last week’s IPO.

Monday aside, AI stocks had already sold off sharply throughout November on worries about profitability and the vast sums pumped into the sector.

By noon in New York, the tech-heavy Nasdaq had shed 2.3% and the broader-based S&P 500 lost 1.1%, while the Dow was just into the green.

Europe’s main stock markets, which feature far fewer tech companies than their Asian and US rivals, finished a handful of percentage points lower after jumping Monday in line with Wall Street.

Huang had resigned less than two weeks ago over extramarital affairs, reportedly with an alleged Chinese spy as well as a senior Nvidia executive before Donald Trump noisily declared he should be brought back.

“Jensen’s return takes away one of the biggest unknowns hanging over the AI trade,” said Charu Chanana, an investment strategist at Saxo Markets.

“He is not just Nvidia’s CEO; he is arguably the biggest salesman for the entire AI ecosystem. His relationships with customers, suppliers and capital providers are difficult to replicate,” she said.

But “Jensen Huang alone cannot support the AI trade in the long term,” said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

“Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session,” she added.

Analysts were in broad agreement that Huang’s return did not mean an end to investigations or the uncertainty that has clouded the AI trade for six months.

The company remains under scrutiny from investigators including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill for allegedly helping Chinese firms gain access to Nvidia’s top-line chips.

FinanceTab.title: EU to impose cap on Chinese hybrid EV imports next month
FinanceTab.text:
The EU will next month impose its threatened caps on the number of Chinese hybrid cars that can be imported into the bloc, the European Commission has announced.

The quotas will also apply to hybrids from Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the UK, but the principal purpose is to limit imports from China after an agreement with Beijing in October that has led to a rise in exports to the bloc.

The quota, under World Trade Organization rules, is temporary and will apply for 200 days from 1 December during an investigation into imports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid vehicles. The EU is attempting to cut its huge trade deficit with China.

“In view of the sensitivity of the hybrids sector, its strategic importance to the union economy in terms of innovation, electrification and employment, and the existence of sufficient evidence showing that imports of hybrids threaten to cause serious injury to the union industry,” the official journal said on Tuesday.

It will limit tariff-free imports of Chinese vehicles to 350,000 in the first year or about 191,000 over 200 days.

First-year quotas would be set at 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK, which last year exported 166,000 hybrids to the EU.

The quota amounts to about half of the number of Chinese hybrids expected to be imported to the EU in the next 12 months.

Figures in the journal showed that imports of Chinese EVs rocketed from 21,000 units in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024 when tariffs were imposed.

After the tariffs were imposed, imports of EVs began to “flatten out”, with a “clear shift” from EVs to hybrids from China, it said.

Worldwide exports of hybrids from China rocketed from 191,000 vehicles in 2023 to 1.124m in 2025, the EU said.

To head off “the likelihood of substantially increased imports into the union”, the EU now is imposing a quota.

The volume limits are “safeguard” measures that have to apply to all big exporters of ‌hybrid cars to the EU. Other countries to which the import caps apply are South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Serbia and the US, but they are most restrictive for China.

According to industry reports, non-EU countries including the UK have questioned the allocations.

At a WTO goods council meeting last week, South Korea questioned whether the investigation was fair and transparent. Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Turkey stressed transparency and due process.

China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by the consensus the two sides had reached, and that it reserved all rights to firmly safeguard the legitimate interests of Chinese industries.

The European Commission said imports from China came not just at the expense of EU production, but were also eating into the market shares of other exporters such as Japan and South Korea.

FinanceTab.title: Wild stock market swings: will I lose money, and is there anything I can do?
FinanceTab.text:
Will I lose money?

Lots of people own shares that are falling in value, either through their pension or other type of investment account. Many of the shares that are experiencing the biggest falls are companies that have dominated indices and, as a result, the passive funds that track them.

Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, says two of the most popular passive investments among investors are global equity funds and funds tracking the S&P 500 US stock market index. “Both have exposure to the giants of tech in a large way,” he says. And, as a result, both have fallen in recent days.

Coatsworth says that, while 15 years ago US shares represented half of the MSCI World index – a benchmark for the global stock market – it is now 73%. Tech is the dominant sector and officially represents 30% of the index. However, Google’s parent Alphabet and Facebook’s owner Meta are classed as communication services stocks – adding them bumps up tech to about 35% of the index.

Investors who think they have diversified by being in a global fund may be having a nasty surprise.

The investment platform interactive investor (ii) reports on the top holdings of its customers every quarter. Its most recent report shows global tracker funds are well-represented in their portfolios, as is Scottish Mortgage – an actively managed investment trust that holds shares in SpaceX, Nvidia and Anthropic, among others.

However, an important thing to remember about falling share prices is that you do not lose money until you sell. Only at that point do you crystallise your loss.

And you may not even have losses on paper, depending on when you invested. In recent years stock markets have been climbing. The FTSE 100 is still higher than it was last year. Scottish Mortgage has been falling since mid-October, but its shares are still well up on this time last year.

How do I diversify to avoid further tech downturns?

Coatsworth says there are a few paths to consider.

“One way to dial down tech exposure is to switch into a global equity fund that excludes the US,” he says. “For example, iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.”

Tech stocks outside the US account for 10.9% of the portfolio, but the main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners. “That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat,” he says. However, if those stocks recover, you will be missing out on any potential gains.

He says a possible “middle ground” is the Invesco MSCI World Equal Weight ETF. At the end of September, the US represented 40.6% of the investment – less than with a traditional global equity fund. “The investor still has their toe in the pond for US tech exposure, but they wouldn’t be up to their neck in the water,” he says.

FinanceTab.title: Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says
FinanceTab.text:
Invoking Greek mythology, the US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, by which the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders were either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.
