articles.title: Meta's Muse has launched in the UK. I found it helpful but awkward
articles.text:
I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.

Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."

And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.

How well Muse works really matters to Meta.

It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.

But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.

"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".

Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.

"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.

"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.

It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.

And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.

Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.

I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.

It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

It ended up telling me to book them myself.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.

A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.

The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch., external

"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.

Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike,", external it says in its press release.

I called my agent Linda - after the robot in the BBC TV series Ann Droid - but it can take any form you like. I gave it a British, female accent from the myriad of choices available.

Linda is proactive. As soon as an email came in, it would summarise it for me and suggest a reply. Sometimes a long time before I was actually ready to respond.

Sometimes, if I hadn't interacted with it for a while, generally because I was busy, it would pop up with some random prompt like "did you know you can change my outfit?" I expect this is designed to drive engagement: Muse is only free to use until a certain point, and then subscriptions kick in.

It also wrote some embarrassing replies to messages on my behalf: in response to a question about whether I would like to go on an outing, for example, it included all the logistics I would need in order to get there, not realising that sometimes "yes, that sounds great" is enough.

It seemed to want to have the last word quite a bit, occasionally getting stuck in a loop of "okay" and "thank you's".

Meta is relying on people choosing to trust it with even more of their personal data, despite a rather dubious track record historically with its social networks and a growing backlash against AI in general.

I asked Linda - my new dedicated if occasionally clunky assistant - if it wanted to take people's jobs. "I'm here to take the admin and the fiddly bits off your plate," it replied, leaving me to do the "thinking".

"Everything you do is stuff I would usually think about," I responded.

"That's fair and you're right," Linda replied, adding: "The difference, I hope, is that you're still the one deciding what matters and what to do about it."

Which would have been more reassuring if the day before Muse's UK launch, Meta's head of AI Alexandr Wang had not written an essay warning about how difficult it will be for humans to remain in control, external once AI is 1,000 times more intelligent than us.

And Linda is helping fuel that revolution, one calendar invite at a time.

articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.text:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.

Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.

China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.

On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".

The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.

The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.

China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.

Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.

Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.

Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.

Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.

That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.

Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.

Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.

Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take.

The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.

In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.

Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: GTA 6 hacker released on licence with warning 'don't let this happen again'
articles.text:
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.

Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."

The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.

Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.

But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.

Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.

He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.

City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".

He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.

He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.

With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.

He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."

articles.title: San Francisco is enjoying an AI boom, but worries about a crash are growing
articles.text:
Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism – which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness – are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy."

As to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking company owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes – "always a reality in San Francisco" – she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she says.

articles.title: Black Friday 2026: Can ChatGPT and other AI tools find you the best bargains?
articles.text:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

articles.title: BBC and Netflix team up for new CBeebies hub on streamer
articles.text:
The BBC and Netflix are to launch a trial hub on the streaming service next month, featuring 24 CBeebies shows.

Programmes including Hey Duggee, Numberblocks and Teletubbies can be seen on a branded CBeebies hub on Netflix from 2 December.

The trial's aim is to test new ways for the flagship pre-school channel to reach audiences. The BBC is the UK's largest commissioner of children's content.

BBC iPlayer will remain the home for all CBeebies content. Some CBeebies shows such as Shaun the Sheep are already available on Netflix, but this is the first time they will have a home hub on the subscription streamer.

CBeebies shows will also be made available to Netflix members outside the UK in a distribution deal managed by BBC Studios, with the aim of driving investment into children's content in the UK. The deal does not include China.

Netflix will also commit to funding a small number of new CBeebies commissions, the BBC said.

BBC's chief content officer Kate Phillips said the corporation is "always looking at how we can help more audiences discover" its content and brands.

"This limited trial will make a curated selection of CBeebies programmes available on Netflix, while BBC iPlayer remains the home of the full CBeebies experience," she added.

Anne Mensah, vice president of Netflix's UK content said the "unique partnership allows us to work hand in hand with the BBC to support our brilliant British kids' programme makers".

She added: "We want to build a fun and safe space parents can feel good about, with content their kids will love."

articles.title: First Children's Booker prize reveals shortlist ' full of surprises' - and its child judges
articles.text:
The first ever Children's Booker Prize has announced the eight books in the running for the new £50,000 award.

Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated collection of short stories are on the shortlist, which is aimed at children aged eight to 12.

The authors in contention include former Children's Laureate of Ireland Eoin Colfer, who is best known for his Artemis Fowl series, and teacher and children's author Catherine Bruton.

Four children have also been announced as new judges after a UK-wide competition. Twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire was one of those picked from more than 4,000 entrants.

He told me he was called back into school for a phone call with chair of judges Frank Cottrell-Boyce, who broke the news. Ibrahim said he couldn't be happier.

"First Children's Booker Prize judge! On my CV - that's going to take me a long way… I'm too overwhelmed to even be excited."

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC "it's really, really important that this is a prize for children's books. Having judges who are children will be proof of that… If the children don't love a book, it won't win."

Ibrahim, his fellow child judges and Cottrell-Boyce will be joined on the judging panel by Ghosts and Horrible Histories actor Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, who owns an award-winning children's book shop in north London.

Ibrahim said he loves reading "because it's just a way to unwind yourself from the outside world. If you get stuck in a book, you're not getting your face out of there until you finish it".

He's far too professional to share which books on the list he likes best, but he told me when he was reading one of them recently: "I had to tell my mum to confiscate it because I couldn't stop reading it and I was getting a headache."

Cottrell-Boyce said he isn't concerned over whether the adult judges might dominate the decision-making.

"If - like me - you've been visiting schools as a children's writer for 20 years, it's a rare thing to meet a child who is too over-awed to express an opinion. They're usually very forthright".

Ibrahim proves that point. He told me "the adults are not going to control that meeting… 100% not!"

He's looking for "something that has different perspectives, you can see it in a different way. New characters, not just the same old sloppy characters that authors make all the time. They just make these books that just have the same plot line".

Cottrell-Boyce told the BBC the range of subjects was "amazing".

"Children's books can be about anything, can deal with anything. But the tone has to convey hope. I can't think of a darker childhood than the one endured by Anne of Green Gables. I also can't think of a more joyous book than Anne of Green Gables."

He acknowledges the worrying statistics on reading. The National Literacy Trust's Annual Literacy Survey last year showed the percentage of children and young people who said they enjoyed reading was its lowest in 20 years. Just one in three aged eight to 18 said they enjoyed reading in their free time, down by more than a third since 2005.

"That's why we're here! To fight the fight. To make sure our children have as many opportunities as possible to discover how pleasurable, how bonding, how thrilling and enriching and fortifying it can be to slip out of the prison of the present into the infinity of the story."

Ibrahim told me "my friends don't read books at all".

He doesn't try to persuade them. "I let them live their life. I live my life".

But if he were to try to, what would he say?

"Put a timer on your phone, make sure it's blocked and then they'll decide to do something more productive. I might be able to convince them... because it can help you with English, your confidence, and help you build self esteem."

For him, though, the best thing about a book is when it takes him into another world. "If you try to take your head out of it, it makes you think 'oh my god what's going to happen next?'"

The winning book will be announced in February next year at the Young V&A in London. 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books will be given to children who need them most.

articles.title: Dancing with the Stars: Irish reality star Maura Higgins reaches final
articles.text:
Maura Higgins is arguably Love Island's biggest success story.

Since leaving the villa in Majorca, Higgins maintained a high profile in the UK, Ireland and across the Atlantic where she has presented Love Island: Aftersun in the US, and was runner up in The Traitors US.

While she failed to find love with Curtis Pritchard in the 2019 series, she may have picked up a few of the ballroom dancer's moves.

The Irish reality TV star has cha cha cha'd her way to the final of Dancing With the Stars on US television, where she will compete with her professional dance partner Mark Ballas, son of Strictly head judge Shirley Ballas.

From County Longford, there'll be a flavour of Ireland in her dances for the final.

In a video posted to the programme's Instagram page, traditional Irish music can be heard while Higgins and Ballas rehearse.

It will not be the first time on the show Higgins has paid homage to her homeland after she and Ballas performed a Paso Doble to Dropkick Murphy's song I'm Shipping up to Boston.

The former Love Island contestant booked her slot in the finale by earning a perfect 30 out of 30 for her samba and a 29 for her Viennese waltz in last week's semi-final, which saw Grey's Anatomy and Glee star Harry Shum Jr lose the public vote.

The show, hosted by Fresh Prince of Bel-Air star Alfonso Ribeiro and Emmy winning dancer Julianne Hough, features a judging panel of three, made up of Derek Hough, Carrie Ann Inaba and former Strictly Come Dancing regular Bruno Tonioli.

Higgins and Ballas will compete for the Len Goodman Mirrorball trophy.

Goodman, who died in April 2023, had been one of the regular judges on the show, following his 12-year stint on Strictly.

The pair will face off against actress Tatyana Ali, Paralympian Ezra Frech, comedian Connor Wood and Olympic figure skater Amber Glenn.

articles.title: Molly Meldrum: King Charles and Elton John pay tribute to Australian music legend
articles.text:
King Charles and Elton John have paid tribute to Australian music industry legend Molly Meldrum, who died aged 83 after a long illness.

Meldrum's family said he "passed away peacefully" at a hospital in Melbourne in the early hours of Monday morning.

The music promoter and broadcaster, born Ian Alexander Meldrum, helped define the nation's music tastes for decades, championing local artists like INXS and Kylie Minogue and global acts like Abba.

Known for his chaotic demeanour and trademark Stetson hat, he interviewed an array of stars, with the king on Monday calling him "a true giant of the music industry".

Born in Victoria in 1943, Meldrum displayed a love of music from an early age and went on to host the Australian Broadcasting Corporation's music television programme Countdown, and later a segment on variety show Hey Hey, It's Saturday.

Meldrum in 2014 became the first person who was not a recording artist to be inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (Aria) Hall of Fame.

Meldrum lived with an acquired brain injury after falling from a ladder in 2011.

"Affectionately dubbed 'the Guru', Molly was the heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music," a statement from Meldrum's family said.

Among his most famous interviews was a 1977 sit-down with King Charles, in which Meldrum could not calm his jitters.

He stumbled over his lines, declaring: "Your Royal Highness... Oh, oh, I'm sweating like a pig".

King Charles reflected on the infamous interview for Countdown's 40th anniversary special, saying: "There is an old showbusiness saying which warns never to work with animals or children. But nobody prepared me for Molly Meldrum".

On Monday, an aide to the King said he had been "deeply saddened" to hear of Meldrum's death.

"His Majesty's interview with Molly is a moment he and many others will never forget - he hopes that interview will once again raise a few smiles as Australians honour Molly's legacy as a true giant of the music industry."

Elton John - a friend and regular interviewee - paid tribute to him as "an Australian legend and an institution", while pop star Kylie Minogue said she would be turning up the music in his honour.

"As a kid, I watched Molly Meldrum on Countdown every single weekend, in awe of the show and the magic it brought to our little TV in the lounge room."

"He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I'm so grateful for his unwavering love and support."

Australia's Arts Minister Tony Burke said the country had lost an icon: "One of his greatest legacies will be the generations of Australians who grew up with his unmistakable enthusiasm and love of music."

articles.title: Bros announce first tour in a decade
articles.text:
The band Bros have announced their first tour in a decade.

Formed in Camberley, Surrey, in 1986 by twin brothers Matt and Luke Goss alongside Craig Logan, the band had hits including When Will I Be Famous?, Drop The Boy and I Owe You Nothing.

Logan left in 1989 and Bros split three years later, although Matt and Luke Goss reunited in 2017 and have not toured together since.

The 10-date tour in 2027 will include a Wembley Arena show, 38 years after Bros played to 77,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where they became the youngest act to headline the venue at the age of 20.

The pair will perform across November and December in London, Portsmouth, Birmingham, Sheffield, Brighton, Bath, Derby, Glasgow, Newcastle and Manchester.

Bros debut album Push achieved quadruple-platinum status in the UK and reached number one in Japan and New Zealand.

They also had five UK top five singles in 1988, with eight UK Top 10 hits across their career.

Matt Goss went on to pursue a solo career, releasing five albums, and competed on Strictly Come Dancing in 2022.

While Luke Goss turned to acting and appeared in Blade II, Hellboy II: The Golden Army, and Tekken.

articles.title: Don Toliver postpones London O2 arena show after Manchester evacuation
articles.text:
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.

"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.

A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.

Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".

"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".

There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.

Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.

"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.

Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking – it was really distressing."

Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.

"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.

Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.

"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.

Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".

Venues are currently focused on keeping out items – such as explosives – that could cause mass casualties, she added.

articles.title: Iranian authorities flog singer who performed without hijab, lawyers say
articles.text:
A prominent singer who performed without the mandatory hijab and four members of her band and production team have been flogged by Iranian authorities, lawyers say.

Parastoo Ahmadi, three musicians and a producer were each given 74 lashes in the city of Qom, a member of their defence team told the BBC.

Ahmadi, 29, wore a sleeveless dress during a concert that was livestreamed in December 2024. Iran's laws ban public performances by women and require them to wear headscarves and modest clothing.

This June, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of "offending public decency" through the publication of "obscene and indecent material", which they had denied.

In addition to being sentenced to 74 lashes, they were banned from audiovisual activities and from leaving the country for two years.

At the end of September, an appeals court in Qom rejected the defendants' appeal and confirmed the sentence, her lawyers said.

There was widespread condemnation of the sentences from other Iranian artists and human rights activists, who warned that flogging constituted cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment, and violated the international prohibition on torture.

On Monday, one of the defendants' lawyers told the BBC that Ahmadi and four of her male co-defendants had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom.

"We did everything in our power to have the verdict overturned, or at least to secure a reduction in the sentence or a suspension, but it didn't work out," he said.

"The other lawyers and I even tried to get the enforcement of the sentence postponed, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately."

Pro-reform daily Etemad cited another defence lawyer, Mostafa Nili, as identifying the four men flogged alongside Ahmadi as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari.

"Parastoo Ahmadi's flogging for singing and dressing as she chooses is a flagrant violation of her fundamental rights and a chilling demonstration of the Iranian authorities' determination to suppress women's freedoms and to violently punish anyone who dares to challenge their discriminatory laws and policies," said Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI).

Under Iranian law, which is based on the country's interpretation of Sharia, women and girls above the age of puberty must cover their hair with a hijab and wear long, loose-fitting clothing to disguise their figures.

In 2022, protests swept across the Islamic Republic following the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman who was detained by morality police in Tehran in September that year for allegedly wearing her hijab "improperly".

Women burnt their headscarves or waved them in the air at the nationwide demonstrations against the clerical establishment, during which hundreds of people were killed in a crackdown by security forces.

Since then, many women and girls have stopped covering their hair in public altogether in open defiance of the dress code. Authorities have responded with periodic waves of arrests, warnings, business closures and other measures.

In January this year, thousands of people were killed and tens of thousands were arrested when security forces crushed another wave of mass anti-establishment protests, this time sparked by the country's economic crisis.

Since the start of Iran's war with the US and Israel in late February, authorities have intensified their use of the death penalty against protesters.

According to the Norway-based group Iran Human Rights, at least 39 men convicted over January's protests and two convicted over the 2022 unrest have been executed, along with 16 people allegedly affiliated with banned opposition groups and 17 others convicted of espionage or collaborating with foreign states.

Another 121 protesters detained in January, including six women and five juvenile offenders, have been sentenced to death and are at imminent risk of execution, it says.

articles.title: Princess Catherine's cancer documentary makes me feel less alone, says Strictly's Amy Dowden
articles.text:
Strictly Come Dancing's Amy Dowden says the upcoming documentary from Catherine, the Princess of Wales, about her cancer journey will help many people, including herself, "not feel so alone".

Dowden praised the documentary and said it confirmed how "anyone can be dealt the devastating blow of a cancer diagnosis".

Dowden, Strictly's first Welsh professional dancer, was diagnosed with stage 3 breast cancer at 32 and has undergone chemotherapy and two mastectomies.

Catherine's BBC documentary, Heal, will reveal how cancer has impacted her outlook on life, as well as the people, places and experiences that have helped her.

Dowden told ITV's Lorraine she believed the documentary would be "quite raw" and emotional, but "so important" in showing the "truth and effects of cancer".

The dancer said she had a lot of admiration for the princess, adding: "Thank you Princess Catherine for doing this."

In the trailer for her documentary, Catherine is candid about life-altering effect of the disease, saying: "Cancer does change you."

"It changes your body, it changes you physically... but there is a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you."

Dowden has previously echoed this feeling, saying that after a diagnosis, "in a click of the fingers, your life changes".

"You have everything stripped away from you," she said.

Heal will follow Catherine as she does the National Three Peaks challenge, which involves climbing the highest mountains in England, Scotland, and Wales within 24 hours.

Catherine completed the challenge in June to raise funds for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, the hospital where she underwent treatment, and to "explore life beyond diagnosis".

When the princess revealed she had cancer, Dowden shared her sympathy on Instagram.

Since her own diagnosis in 2023, the dancer has shared her experience of breast cancer online and in the BBC documentary Strictly Amy: Cancer and Me.

She said her decision to let a camera crew film her cancer journey was scary, but she felt a duty to raise awareness.

"I felt straight away, well maybe I could make a difference."

Like Catherine, Dowden's cancer is in remission, and she has been performing in the current series of Strictly.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
articles.text:
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.

A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.

Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.

Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.

In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.

The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.

Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.

The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.

Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.

articles.title: Russell Brand's wife says she'll honour prison rules after message row
articles.text:
The wife of disgraced comedian Russell Brand says she will "honour" the rules of his prison, a week after she read a message from her husband proclaiming his innocence.

Laura Brand, 39, drew criticism from ministers after reading out the message from inside HMP Littlehey last week, prompting the government to seek to have the episode removed from social media platforms.

She said on Sunday that she would continue to defend her family and herself over her portrayal in the media during the couple's weekly podcast, which she now presents alone.

Russell Brand, 51, is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

"Last week's episode drew a considerable amount of attention," Laura Brand said during this week's episode of Sunday Service.

"Now that I understand the parameters set by the brilliant and professional staff at HMP Littlehey, I will absolutely honour that."

In the relayed message last week, Russell Brand had said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".

Laura Brand said she had spoken to him at the Cambridgeshire prison and said he was "OK".

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

Further allegations have since been reported about him and some have called for consent laws to be revised.

His conviction has renewed conversation about safeguarding in the media industry, and whether some celebrities are still able to use their fame to prey on women and then silence them.

Ministers have pointed out that inmates are prohibited from making statements that are likely to cause their victims distress and have said Brand's message was being investigated.

A woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16, but who was not among the women whose accusations led to his conviction, said his prison message was "upsetting" and "really shocking".

The government attempted to have the podcast removed from YouTube, but this was refused by its owner Google. Prime Minister Andy Burnham urged social media companies to "show some decency and take these videos down".

On Sunday, Laura Brand also said that Sunday Service would be a place where she would "continue to be proud to be a wife, a mother and a woman defending her family at a time when the media's image of what kind of a woman I am is under so much scrutiny".

She expressed feeling a mixture of "grief", "absence", "desolation" and "loneliness" since her husband's imprisonment.

articles.title: Strictly Come Dancing noise disruption prompts BBC apology
articles.text:
The BBC has apologised "for any offence caused" after lewd audio was heard during the live broadcast of Strictly Come Dancing.

A recording of sex noises appeared to be playing from the audience in Blackpool's Tower Ballroom as judge Motsi Mabuse gave feedback early in Saturday's episode. She paused before joking: "It's not me."

At the end of the programme, presenter Emma Willis apologised to viewers "if you heard any audio disruptions". A BBC spokesperson also issued an apology and said it was "investigating how this happened".

Lancashire police said it was assessing whether any criminal offences may have taken place, after receiving a formal complaint and a mobile phone being seized.

The moment was streamed on social media by content creator Daniel Jarvis, whose videos include pranks. He appeared to place a phone call before the audio began playing in the ballroom, and suggested he was trying to target judge Craig Revel Horwood for his "bullying".

Jarvis has previously claimed he was responsible for sex noises disrupting Match of the Day in 2023.

Willis told viewers: "Before we see the judges' leaderboard, we'd like to apologise if you heard any audio disruptions earlier in tonight's show and for any offence caused."

articles.title: ‘The Terence Conran of his day’: the visionary Victorian futurist adored by design superstars today
articles.text:
Victorian industrial designer Christopher Dresser was always a visionary. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked.

But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since.

Using his ideas on botanical form, he created designs strikingly at odds with the aesthetic of the times. He took the everyday – teapots, toast racks and pitchers – and made them unfamiliar and futuristic. But his achievements are now not widely known.

“Everyone knows about William Morris and the Arts and Craft movement,” says Ian Robinson, a collector of Dresser’s work. “Morris’s politics kept him in with the era’s movers and shakers, and subsequently on the radars of curators and historians. But Dresser was focused on technological developments and using mass production to bring design to every home, which didn’t sound as sexy. It’s interesting how history plays out in these stories. Dresser was embracing new methods; Morris was looking backwards.”

A new exhibition, Christopher Dresser: The Pursuit of Beauty at the Hub, a centre for craft and design in Sleaford, hopes to reinstate the designer’s legacy with a survey of his modernist ceramics, fluid glassware and sharply angular metalwork.

“Ask your friends if they’ve heard of Christopher Dresser, and nine times out of 10 they’ll say no,” says Joshua Lockwood, exhibitions manager and curator at the Hub. Robinson, who has lent work to the exhibition, is such a Dresser fan that he’s got one eye on an online auction for a piece while we talk on a video call.

“If I show people his designs, they recognise some pieces, such as the sugar bowl that Italian design brand Alessi brought back into production in the 1990s, but they don’t know who made them,” Robinson says. “He was the Terence Conran of his day, but he’s not remembered.”

Dresser was born in Glasgow and studied structure and science at the Government School of Design (later renamed the Royal College of Art) under influential academics architect Owen Jones and art critic Gottfried Semper. He became professor of artistic botany there himself, but after missing out on the chair of botany at London University in 1860, Dresser ditched academia and worked instead as a consultant for businesses such as Wedgwood pottery, Minton’s porcelain, Liberty of London and Tiffany & Co.

He created an experimental body of work, remarkable in terms of technology and influence. In his metalwork, Dresser experimented with unusual metal alloys and then cutting-edge processes such as electroplating to make exceptionally sleek household objects. He was co-founder and art director at Linthorpe Art Pottery, a revolutionary workshop set up in 1879 that was the first in the country to use gas-powered kilns. This innovation let Dresser develop his signature mottled glazes, and he designed over 1,000 vessels in the three years he worked there.

He travelled to Japan in 1876 on behalf of the South Kensington Museum (now the V&A), and helped start the Victorian craze for Japonisme. “That was his thing, to bring beautiful things to the home,” says Robinson. “He wanted to bring good design to as many people as possible. To buy Morris’s furniture you had to be very wealthy. Dresser mainly worked in silverplate or even painted tin. It was beautiful design but it was also affordable.”

Dresser’s family tried to continue his design studio after his death in 1904, but when that proved unsuccessful they disposed of all his account books and drawings, effectively destroying his archive. “I think they burned everything,” says Robinson. “All the documents were lost and it wasn’t until the 1970s that anyone started looking into his work again.”

Designers Philippe Starck, Terence Conran and Alberto Alessi have all expressed admiration for Dresser’s ability to bridge great design, mass production and respect for the middle-class consumer; and artists such as ceramicist Magdalene Odundo and sculptor Alice Channer have been influenced by the sleek, sinuous botanical shapes that define his work. Odundo saw Dresser’s ceramics at the British Museum as a student, and was inspired by the way he pulled ideas together to create something new, rather than to emulate what already exists. Her work will also be on show at the Hub alongside Channer and artists Coco Crampton and Gabriele Beveridge.

“Hopefully this exhibition will bring more awareness of Dresser,” says Lockwood. “Not just his production of objects but that his work has lineage. This history hasn’t really been told and I want to bring this wonderful designer to the forefront.”
